sources.news_title: Trump signs order to reduce childhood vaccines and break up MMR shots
sources.text:
Trump signs order to reduce childhood vaccines and break up MMR shots
US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order calling for American children to be immunised against fewer diseases.
The vaccination schedule put forward by his administration recommends immunising children against 11 diseases, six fewer than what is currently recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Doctors say the order is based on pseudoscience, and will harm children.
Here's what to know about the order.
So, what are changes?
In short, the revised schedule called for by Mr Trump seeks to reduce the number of diseases and viruses American parents are advised to vaccinate their children against.
The six vaccinations the Trump administration would drop from the routine childhood immunisation schedule are:
- RSV
- Hepatitis A
- Hepatitis B
- Meningococcal ACWY
- Rotavirus
- Influenza
The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate, single-disease shots, despite scientific consensus that the combined shot is safe and effective.
It also directs the nation's health department to improve research on vaccines, which are already extensively studied.
Why did he order the changes?
The changes appear to be motivated by misinformation, public health experts say.
In signing the order, Mr Trump promoted his long-held but discredited theory that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
That's despite public health experts raising concerns that spacing out shots in such a way could lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
Childhood vaccines (and how and when to give them in combination) go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Kush Desai, a spokesperson for the president, told the Associated Press the plan to develop single-disease vaccines would "give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children", and increase vaccine uptake.
Mr Trump also repeatedly suggested the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.
But scientific consensus based on decades of studies firmly concludes that there is no link.
Secretary of Health Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine critic, also said American children get 72 shots under the current schedule.
But that number includes vaccines administered during pregnancy and individual components of combined shots that inoculate against several diseases.
The schedule currently recommended by the CDC is similar to those in Australia, the UK and Canada.
The Royal Australian College of GPs Specific Interests Child and Young Person's Health chair, Tim Jones, said the announcement would increase harm to children.
He disputed Mr Trump's recommendations, which he told the ABC were informed by pseudoscience and would "muddy the waters on the safety and effectiveness of childhood immunisation".
"He is harming infants who have no ability to advocate for their own health by continuing to peddle harmful, unsubstantiated claims at parents,"
Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, also slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.
"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong," the Louisiana senator wrote.
"Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.
"The president does not have the expertise to make these changes."
WHO spokesperson Tarik Jašarević told a press briefing in Geneva that vaccination recommendations were based on more than 60 years of research by WHO, national authorities and independent expert groups.
"What comes out from WHO is science-based," Mr Jašarević said.
"We hope that all countries will use this best scientific evidence that we have."
Can Trump change vaccine policy?
It's not exactly clear.
In the US, vaccination recommendations are approved by the CDC director on the advice of a committee of experts.
Mr Trump ordered the Department of Health and Human Services in December to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising US guidelines.
The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, but that move was later blocked in court.
That ruling was part of an ongoing lawsuit brought by medical organisations that argued the Trump administration did not follow standard legal procedure.
But Lawrence Gostin, a public health law expert at Georgetown University, said the Supreme Court's interpretation of Mr Trump's power may allow him to supersede CDC director Erica Schwartz if she does not agree to the new recommendations.
"This is clearly the first test for Dr Erica Schwartz," he said.
"The president is placing her in an untenable position."
What about vaccine mandates?
In most US states, children must be immunised against certain diseases to attend day care or enrol in school.
That's not something the president has the authority to change.
In fact, the executive order only advises states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration's preferred schedule, according to a White House fact sheet.
Are there concerns about vaccine uptake?
Yes.
Doctors have raised concerns that the Trump administration's misinformation around vaccines could stoke vaccine hesitancy.
Mr Trump's executive order comes as students are returning to classrooms after their summer breaks.
Federal data shows US kindergarten vaccination rates have been dropping, with the share of children with exemptions rising to an all-time high in the 2024-25 school year.
The nation is contending with a measles outbreak so severe, experts say it could result in the US losing its measles elimination status.
Dr Jones said the outbreak has so far impacted more than 2,400 Americans, almost all of whom were unvaccinated, and caused three deaths.
Medical experts have linked the rise to slumping vaccination rates, a trend many attribute in part to vaccine scepticism espoused by Mr Kennedy.
Just this month, Mr Kennedy urged parents to vaccinate their children against measles, though he took no responsibility for the surge.
Mr Trump's executive order would needlessly contribute to increased fear and avoidance of vaccination both in the US and around the world, Dr Jones added.
"Without confidence in the lifesaving properties of widespread vaccination of children further children are going to die of preventable diseases — a travesty."
ABC/AP

sources.news_title: Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine regimen, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine
sources.text:
Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine regimen, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California. (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Monday signed a sweeping executive order that aims to reshape guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, standing alongside Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and was met with immediate pushback.
The order — which calls on federal programs and funding to “support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines” — came as Trump continued to erroneously connect vaccines with autism during the White House event and his administration has sought to de-emphasize childhood vaccinations’ importance.
“This updated recommendation finally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world,” Trump said during a signing ceremony in the Oval Office, joined by Kennedy, a longtime opponent of vaccines, as well as National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya and “Make America Healthy Again” advocate Jayme Franklin, also founder and CEO of The Conservateur lifestyle brand, and others.
“More importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge,” Trump added.
Moore administration wants health secretary to issue vaccine recommendations, apart from feds
What the order can legally accomplish was unclear as it’s up to states to decide which recommendations to follow.
GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, rebutted the new order on social media. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy said. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”
Splitting up MMR vaccine
The order recognizes “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” and divides the childhood immunization recommendations into three categories.
The order recommends all children receive immunizations for 11 diseases, including for “measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella.”
Immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations include: “respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.”
The order also lists “hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza, and COVID-19” as immunizations “based on shared clinical decision-making.”
Trump’s executive order also calls for splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and recommends that “all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.” Such single-disease shots are not currently available in the United States, White House officials acknowledged on a background call, but said they believe work will occur in the private sector to make that option eventually available.
“For example, at one year, you should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than getting them all in the same day,” Trump said during the signing ceremony.
Trump said the order also directs the attorney general “to advance legal challenges against states that violate children’s rights to religious or medical vaccination exemptions.”
‘Uncertainty and fear and confusion’
Meanwhile, Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, told reporters Monday during a press briefing after the Trump event that “the only thing that I can see is going to happen as a result of the announcement from today is an injection of greater amounts of uncertainty and fear and confusion, when there doesn’t need to be any of that.”
Many states rely on the AAP, rather than the federal government, for guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, according to the health research organization KFF, following earlier moves on vaccines during the Trump administration.
Rep. Frank Pallone, ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, blasted Trump’s order, saying the effort “lets political appointees attempt to overrule decades of peer-reviewed science and dictate vaccine schedules to American families,” in a statement.
The New Jersey Democrat added that “parents deserve accurate, trusted medical guidance, not a White House-curated list designed to rubberstamp Secretary Kennedy’s radical anti-vaccine agenda.”
Democrats from a coalition of states filed suit earlier this year over Trump administration changes to the federal vaccine guidelines, as did medical groups, but White House officials said Trump’s recommendations were not related to the litigation and were within his authority.

sources.news_title: US Health Secretary R.F.Kennedy Jr. gets his way as Trump order reduces US vaccine schedule
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive ordercalling for fewer childhood vaccinations by limiting the inoculation schedule to 11 immunizations, which he said would give U.S. children “gold-standard” protection and align the country with peer nations that recommend fewer shots.
The order advances a long-standing goal of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an anti-vaccine activist who has promoted a link between vaccines and autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.
“Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold-standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up,” Trump said during a White House signing ceremony where he repeatedly cited a growing number of U.S. autism diagnoses.
“There are some groups that have virtually no problem with autism,” Trump said. “They’re groups that aren’t big into the world of vaccines, so there is something wrong.”
Physicians roundly rejected the action, saying no new science warranted a change, and that the U.S. schedule reflects decades of evidence and the specific health needs of Americans, rejecting the comparison to other countries. Fewer recommended shots will leave more children exposed to preventable diseases, they said.
The order also recommends splitting the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots taken at separate visits.
Kennedy in January cut the U.S. immunization schedule to remove shots against six out of 17 diseases, a move halted by a federal court ruling. The executive order says it reaffirms Kennedy’s overhaul despite the ongoing litigation.
Existing coverage under the Vaccines for Children program relied on by many families will continue, a senior administration official said. The government-funded program provides vaccines for those who may not be able to afford them.
The order directs the Justice Department to challenge state vaccination laws, escalating a federal fight over school immunization requirements set by states. It instructs the attorney general to sue over state laws the administration says conflict with parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations and equal protection, including rules on religious and medical exemptions from immunization mandates.
HEALTH EXPERTS REJECT CHANGES
Medical associations, public health experts, and vaccine makers also criticized the order.
The main outcome would be “confusion for parents,” said Dr. Aaron Milstone of the American Academy of Pediatrics Committee on Infectious Diseases. Conflicting messages, he added, would likely lead parents to delay vaccination.
Merck said there is no published scientific evidence showing any benefit to splitting the MMR shot into three, and that using the individual components increases injections and can lead to delayed or missed immunizations.
Dr. Elizabeth Mack, a pediatric critical care physician in Charleston, South Carolina, said no licensed single-antigen measles, mumps or rubella vaccines were available in the United States, making the recommendation unfeasible as written.
“We don’t have a system that supports this,” she said, questioning whether extra visits would be required and if they would be reimbursed by insurers.
Mike Ybarra, chief medical officer of pharmaceutical lobby group PhRMA, said the schedule was built on decades of rigorous research and any changes “should be driven by the same high standard of evidence.”
The order was also criticized by Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician who chairs the Senate health committee and shepherded Trump’s health agency nominees through, casting the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-endorsed challenger and will leave office in January, said in a statement.
ADMINISTRATION CLAIMS CHALLENGED
Trump, Kennedy and other officials said the order means U.S. children would receive far fewer than the 72 injections recommended under the previous schedule.
Vaccine experts say that figure is inflated, because it counts combination shots such as MMR as multiple injections, and assumes annual flu and COVID-19 doses. Other developed countries that may recommend fewer shots face different disease risks and have different healthcare systems.
Kennedy said health agencies had numerous efforts underway including a new initiative focused on the “foundational causes and biology of autism.”
AAP President Dr. Andrew Racine called the administration’s plans to again look for a link between vaccines and autism misguided, adding that 40 well-designed studies had already examined the question over a long period of time and found no link.
“The issue is not that the science isn’t done. The science is done,” said Dr. Alycia Halladay, chief science officer at the Autism Science Foundation. “The issue is that some people choose not to believe what the studies clearly show because the results don’t conform to their beliefs.”

sources.news_title: Trump cuts childhood vaccine recommendations, draws medical concern
sources.text:
Aug. 10 (UPI) — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday to reduce the number of vaccines recommended for children, sparking widespread concern among the medical community.
At the signing of the executive order during an Oval Office press conference, Trump shared without evidence widely debunked claims that childhood vaccines are linked to an increase in autism diagnoses. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was present for the signing, has maintained this stance as well.
Scientific research into potential links between vaccines and autism has consistently found no connection.
Trump’s executive order also advises breaking up MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, which Trump called “quite lethal,” into three separate vaccines. In the more than 50 years since the MMR vaccine was developed, there has been no evidence that it is deadly.
“Nothing bad can happen from what we’re doing,” Trump said.
Vaccine advocates and researchers have warned that reducing childhood vaccine recommendations will make children more vulnerable to disease. Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who is a medical doctor, posted on social media that the executive order “is wrong.”
“The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy wrote. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.”
Major U.S. medical associations and American doctors were quick to rebuke the executive order as a rejection of science at a time when the United States is experiencing its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades.
“At a time when communities across the country are confronting the return of preventable diseases, the nation should be strengthening its ability to protect children, not putting that progress at risk,” the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases said in a statement.
The American Medical Association criticized the executive order, stating, “decisions about how and when vaccines are used should be driven by rigorous scientific evidence, patient safety and independent medical and public health expertise.”
“Altering a proven vaccination schedule without credible evidence risks weakening public confidence and putting children’s health at risk,” AMA President Willie Underwood said in a statement.
The American College of Physicians said the executive order was “part of a troubling pattern” by the Trump administration to unilaterally change vaccine guidance without relying on “the transparent, scientific review that has guided the U.S. childhood vaccine schedule for decades.”
“If implemented, the changes could increase costs to patients and families, including additional copays while also placing a greater burden on families needing to schedule multiple appointments for a multiple-dose MMR vaccine,” ACP President Jan Carney said in a statement.
“ACP asserts that these changes cannot be allowed to move forward. We must employ as many proven evidence-based methods as possible to ensure sufficient access to vaccines to protect precious lives.”
Trump acknowledged the increased burden of breaking up vaccines when addressing reporters after the signing.
“It’s inconvenient. It’s five stops but it’s something that I think will have a huge impact on autism,” Trump said.

sources.news_title: What parents need to know about Trump's executive order overhauling childhood vaccines
sources.text:
BAKERSFIELD, Calif. (KERO) — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday overhauling the way childhood vaccines are recommended, including a plan to eventually offer the MMR vaccine as three separate shots.
The order directs the federal government to move toward separating the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella. Standalone vaccines for each disease are not currently available in the U.S. The administration says it wants those options developed while also keeping the combined MMR vaccine available.
The combined MMR vaccine remains available, and the executive order does not require parents to separate their child's MMR shots.
Trump said at the signing:
"Today, we're proud to officially announce the United States of America's gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. And that has to do with many subjects, but including autism in particular."
The order also recommends that childhood vaccines be given during separate medical visits. Some public health experts have raised concerns that requiring more appointments could make it easier for families to miss vaccinations, leaving children unprotected for longer.
The administration is also changing which vaccines are routinely recommended for children. Some, including polio, tetanus, HPV and chickenpox, remain recommended for all children. Others, including some hepatitis and RSV immunizations, are now recommended only for certain high-risk groups.
Vaccines including the flu shot and COVID-19 vaccine are moved into a category where doctors and patients make the decision together.
The executive order does not change California's school vaccination requirements, which are set by the state. Critics of the changes say they could make it more difficult for children to get vaccinated on time and could create confusion about which vaccines children should receive.
Medical experts continue to say there is no scientific evidence that the MMR vaccine causes autism. I reached out to several local hospitals and physicians, but no one was available for comment.

sources.news_title: Despite no evidence vaccines cause autism, Trump order pushes for overhaul of childhood vaccine schedule
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 — US President Donald Trump signed an executive order yesterday pushing for a rethink of school vaccine mandates and repeating calls for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be separated into three individual shots.
Many medical experts cast the push as scientifically baseless and potentially damaging to public health.
Curbing vaccines has been a key priority for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit and has long promoted a disproven link between immunization and autism.
The federal government does not have direct control over several areas covered by the order. States, for example, have the authority to require vaccinations for students to attend school.
On these points Trump's move is more of a suggestion than an order.
"States and territories are advised to review" the Trump administration's recommendations on "immunisation requirements for contexts such as school enrollment and attendance," the order states.
In another section, it says the US Health and Human Services department will form a task force to offer the MMR shot as individual vaccines "by working with the private sector and other countries as appropriate, while guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines and those vaccines recommended for shared clinical decision-making."
New York City's health commissioner, Alister Martin, said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."
"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said in a statement.
"Cities and states can set their own recommendations and requirements, and many, including New York City, have moved away from the federal government's recommendations as they've become politicized and unscientific."
Years of clinical evidence support the safety of a combined MMR vaccine.

sources.news_title: Trump Executive Order Decreases Number of Childhood Vaccine Recommendations
sources.text:
An executive order to decrease the number of immunizations recommended for children by federal agencies to “maximize parental choice over childhood vaccines” was signed Monday by President Donald Trump, who drew a link between vaccines and the increase in autism diagnoses.
With Trump’s latest order, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) immunization schedule will recommend that children receive vaccines to protect against 11 diseases — down from the 18 diseases recommended by the agency in 2024. From now on, the CDC will recognize the “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” which were put in place with recommendations from health professionals.
Immunizations for hepatitis, COVID-19, and influenza are among the shots that will no longer be recommended for all children, but will still be available if parents opt in.
The MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine will now also be given out in three separate vaccinations at three separate doctor’s visits, as opposed to all at once.
“Together there could be a possibility that they are quite lethal, and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, just very effective,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office of splitting up the MMR shots.
“This updated recommendation vitally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world; more importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge,” the president explained, before addressing the theory that today’s higher rates of autism may be connected to certain childhood vaccines.
According to Trump, the number of autism cases “did not exist” in generations prior, and there is a reason for such an “epidemic” of cases in 2026.
“We’re going to bring it back much closer to where it was,” he said, referring to the number of diagnoses. “While we do not know what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world.”
States that enact school vaccine requirements “are advised to consider the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations and consider updating their laws to reflect the recommendations,” a White House fact sheet states. “All Federal agencies are advised to advance the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations based on their relevant authorities to ensure Americans have the best scientific information.”
A scientific assessment that came before the order found that the United States currently recommends more childhood vaccines than any peer nation — more than twice as many doses as some European nations.
The assessment also found that most peer nations maintain high childhood vaccination rates through public trust and education, rather than mandates.
During the signing, Trump gave credit to medical professionals including Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Heidi Overton, a medical doctor who serves as the deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy.
He also thanked Jayme Franklin, a “MAHA mom” and political commentator known for founding the Conservateur.
The order also directs the HHS secretary to “present plans to the President to improve vaccine research and options for American parents, including continuous evaluation of the risk and benefit profiles of all childhood vaccines based on U.S. and international data.”
Monday’s announcement and signing marks a “major victory for parents’ rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard in science,” Trump noted.
When questioned on why the establishment media seems to be “against even asking questions about vaccines” by Breitbart News’s Nick Gilbertson, the president blamed Big Pharma companies.
“It’s amazing […] It could be the medical groups, the pharmaceutical groups, I don’t know. But it is amazing. There’s nothing that we lose with this,” Trump told Gilbertson. “The worst thing that would happen would be nothing happens. We’re not going to lose anything. At the same time, we could gain tremendously.”
“We could save hundreds of thousands of lives, millions of lives,” the president continued. “And I wish we could have done that a long time ago,” he added, noting that the process had been held up by a Massachusetts court. “I believed in this for a long time, so now we’re getting it done, and I think you’re going to see tremendous, potentially tremendous results.”
Olivia Rondeau is a politics reporter for Breitbart News based in Washington, DC. Find her on X/Twitter and Instagram.

sources.news_title: Washington childhood vaccine rules not changing, state health leaders say
sources.text:
SEATTLE — Washington's school requirements around childhood vaccines have not changed, state health officials said Monday in response to President Donald Trump's latest efforts to revamp immunization practices in the country.
In a new executive order, Trump calls for scaling back the number of childhood shots recommended by the federal government, and separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different immunizations. Both moves — which come less than a month before the start of the new school year — have been widely criticized by public health experts, including in the Pacific Northwest, who point to years of research backing the MMR shots and timing of the current childhood vaccine schedule.
States have the authority to require vaccinations for K-12 students, not the federal government. In Washington, requirements and guidance will stay the same for the coming academic year, and are informed by recommendations from "trusted medical and public health experts," the state Department of Health said in a statement Monday, following the president's order.
"As DOH reviews today’s announcement, we encourage people to continue following existing Washington state vaccine guidance to protect themselves and their children, and to go to their health care providers with questions and concerns," the state health department said.
Mike Faulk, spokesperson for state Attorney General Nick Brown, wrote in an email that the office plans to review the order for Washington impacts, but he declined to say whether the state might pursue legal action.
Washington state law requires any child attending school, preschool or childcare to have documentation of immunity (through vaccination or proof of acquired immunity) against 11 diseases, ranging from chickenpox to whooping cough.
In January, when the CDC reduced the number of routine vaccines recommended to all U.S. children, Washington and other states in the West Coast Health Alliance endorsed the American Academy of Pediatrics' recommended immunization schedule instead.
Per that schedule, the state health department says children in Washington should get their first MMR dose when they're between 12 and 15 months old, and the second between 4 and 6 years old.
Parents or guardians must fill out a state-approved Certification of Immunization Status form for their child to attend school or childcare.
State law allows parents or guardians to exempt their child from vaccine requirements for personal/philosophical, religious or medical reasons (students may not use a personal exemption for an MMR vaccine in Washington, following a 2019 change).
During the 2025-26 school year, about 95% of K-12 students received their MMR shot — slightly more than last year, according to state health department data. About 90% of kindergartners got their MMR vaccine, roughly the same as the year prior, below the herd-immunity threshold of 95% for measles.
About 2.8% of all children, meanwhile, received exemptions from the MMR shot, a figure that's crept up almost every year since 2019. Among kindergartners, about 4.5% claimed measles, mumps and rubella exemptions.
Trump has repeatedly suggested a link between childhood vaccines and rising rates of autism spectrum disorder, which he did again as he signed the executive order in the Oval Office on Monday. This connection has been widely discredited by public health researchers and scientists who have shown evidence that there is no link between vaccines and autism.

sources.news_title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
sources.text:
Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
August 11, 2026
On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.
The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.
Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."
What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?
The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.
However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.
The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.
Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?
Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.
They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.
Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.
"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.
What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?
Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.
Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.
How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?
Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.
"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."
Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.
New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."
"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.
Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?
The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.
Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.
The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to roll back childhood vaccines
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held but discredited theory that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order advocates separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different single-disease shots and administering all childhood immunisations at separate appointments whenever possible.
It also directs the nation’s health department to improve research on vaccines, which are already extensively studied, and present a plan to offer separate measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines for children, since that is not currently an option in the United States.
Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today
The renewed focus on vaccines marks a departure from the Trump administration’s recent efforts to emphasise less controversial health policies related to healthy eating, drug price negotiations and medical fraud crackdowns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Trump called the announcement a “major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science.”
Speaking about the order at the Oval Office on Monday, Trump repeatedly suggested the number or timing of vaccines could play a role in rising rates of autism spectrum disorder, even as scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link.
The order also includes several changes to the childhood vaccine schedule that his health department has already attempted, but that have been blocked by a federal judge.
A White House official who insisted on anonymity to brief reporters said Trump was within his right to provide his own recommendation through the executive order and said the lawsuit blocking the health department’s schedule was a separate issue.
Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said the announcement spreads uncertainty, fear and confusion where “there doesn’t need to be any of that.”
He disputed Trump’s recommendations and said previous ones should stand.
“Science about vaccines and their efficacy has not changed,” he said.
“The distribution of viruses and other pathogens in our environment has not changed. Children in this country have not changed in the last 48 hours.”
Senator Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee, slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” the Louisiana senator wrote.
“The President does not have the expertise to make these changes.”
Who is in charge of vaccine policy?
Even as the order calls for revised vaccine recommendations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren.
The order advises states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration’s preferred schedule, according to a White House fact sheet.
Last December, Trump ordered the Department of Health and Human Services to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising US guidance accordingly.
The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, a move that has since been blocked in court.
Changes to federal childhood vaccine recommendations customarily require approval from the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The newly Senate-confirmed CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz, oversaw policies promoting vaccination of service members while in a leadership position at the US Coast Guard.
However, public health law expert Lawrence Gostin at Georgetown University said the Supreme Court’s interpretation of Trump’s power may allow him to supersede Schwartz if she does not agree to new recommendations.
“This is clearly the first test for Dr Erica Schwartz,” Gostin said in an email.
“The President is placing her in an untenable position.”
Asked on a call with reporters why the president was advocating splitting MMR into three single-disease vaccines, the White House official did not provide any studies supporting the decision.
They said that was Trump’s long-held view and that some countries provide individual measles vaccines in certain circumstances.
Kush Desai, a Trump spokesperson, told The Associated Press that the president is “one of countless parents who have voiced questions and concerns about the combined MMR vaccine” and said the plan to develop single-disease vaccines would “give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children,” ultimately increasing vaccine uptake.
Studies of babies and toddlers in the US have shown that the use of combination shots for childhood vaccines, rather than single ones, increased the likelihood of completing all recommended vaccinations by the age of two.
Announcement follows other Trump administration vaccine actions
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, an anti-vaccine activist before he entered politics, set out to overhaul immunisation guidance at DHS in the first year of Trump’s term.
He fired an entire 17-member vaccine advisory committee, installing replacements who made far more restrictive recommendations that have since been halted by a federal judge.
He also personally directed the CDC to abandon its position that vaccines do not cause autism, without supplying any new evidence to support the change.
Throughout his second term, Trump has been fixated on connecting autism to vaccines. He has recently ramped up pressure on Kennedy to identify the cause of autism, something Kennedy had pledged to do with new research unveiled last year.
Trump publicly prodded the health secretary for an update on autism research in a Cabinet meeting last month.
“How are you doing on the autism research?” Trump asked.
“We will have an answer for you,” Kennedy said.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between childhood vaccines and autism.
Racine reiterated that point on Monday, noting that the potential link had been studied in “over 40 methodologically well-designed studies in over seven countries involving over 5 million children.”
“I’m not sure that there is anything that has been as thoroughly looked at as this question,” he said.
“And the answer is unequivocally no.”
In the Oval Office, Kennedy repeated his assertion that he believes an unknown environmental factor is to blame for rising autism diagnoses and said that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
Monday’s order comes as students are returning to classrooms around the country and the nation contends with a measles outbreak that experts say could result in the US losing its measles elimination status.
Doctors have raised concerns that Trump’s falsehoods on vaccines could stoke vaccine hesitancy.
Federal data shows US kindergarten vaccination rates have been dropping, with the share of children with exemptions rising to an all-time high in the 2024-25 school year.

sources.news_title: Trump's vaccine order sparks backlash: Doctor opposes splitting MMR shot, says 'this is so wrong'
sources.text:
Trump's vaccine order sparks backlash: Doctor opposes splitting MMR shot, says 'this is so wrong'
President Trump has signed an executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccines and splitting the MMR shot into three separate doses
President Donald Trump’s new childhood vaccine order has triggered a sharp response from doctors and health experts. While the administration says the move will give parents more choice, critics warn that splitting the MMR vaccine could mean more shots and more doctor visits.
Doctors and health experts push back
Senator Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a doctor and chairman of the Senate health committee, strongly criticized the order on X: “I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child's pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong.”
The CDC says there's “no published scientific evidence [that] shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots." It notes there can be a “very small risk” of febrile seizures and extremely rare cases of serious allergic reactions with the MMR vaccine, but that getting it “is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella.” Vaccine safety experts at the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics also agree the MMR shot is not responsible for recent increases in autism diagnoses.
What the executive order says
US President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order stating that his administration would recognize “Gold Standard” recommendations for 11 core childhood vaccinations against serious diseases, along with the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine, as per ANI.
Trump said that for years, the US had recommended more childhood vaccines than other peer nations, with children in some cases receiving up to 72 vaccine doses. “Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing Gold Standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR,” Trump said while signing the order in the Oval Office.
The executive order states that “the combined MMR vaccine should be administered in three separate single-disease shots once such products are domestically available and that, to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.”
Trump also spoke directly about the MMR vaccine at the signing event: “You have the MMR. We want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times.” He suggested the vaccine could be "quite lethal" when given all at once, comparing the volume to "a bottle of soda." He also said, “No parent should feel the pressure of immediately after their child is born, and a bunch of vaccines are pressured and pushed upon them. This is about freedom at the end of the day.”
Also Read: US has revoked over 175k visas amid Trump's immigration crackdown: State Department
What officials in the administration said
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr said the administration would work to ensure vaccine access while also strengthening safety monitoring. “We will preserve access to vaccines, strengthen safety monitoring, expand research, give doctors and parents better information, and restore informed consent and parental choice to their rightful place in American medicine,” he said, as per ANI.
NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya said the move would restore autonomy for families while continuing to emphasize science in vaccine recommendations. “This restores a healthy relationship between public health and parents,” he said.
White House adviser Stephen Miller also backed the decision, saying, “This is an action that ensures the dignity of patients, the dignity of parents. It restores choice and says we are going to let the parent and doctor make a sound medical decision.”
Background on measles and the MMR vaccine
Measles is a highly contagious airborne virus. It can infect up to nine out of ten unvaccinated people who are exposed to it, as per ANI. While most symptoms go away within weeks, the disease can be serious for young children and can lead to problems like ear infections, pneumonia, or encephalitis (brain swelling), which can cause long-term issues like seizures and memory problems.
The MMR vaccine is the only effective way to prevent measles. Doctors recommend the first dose before a child turns 15 months old, and the second dose before age six. The vaccine is considered safe and gives lifelong protection, but vaccination rates have dropped in some countries, including the US, partly due to misinformation.

sources.news_title: Trump Announces Changes to Childhood Vaccine Recommendations, Sets 11 Core Vaccinations as 'Gold Standard'
Trump order reduces US vaccine schedule
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday calling for fewer childhood vaccinations by limiting the inoculation schedule to 11 immunisations, which he said would give US children "gold-standard" protection and align the country with peer nations that recommend fewer shots.
The order advances a long-standing goal of Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, an anti-vaccine activist who has promoted a link between vaccines and autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.
Public health experts say the US schedule reflects decades of evidence and the specific health needs of Americans, and that fewer recommended shots will leave more children exposed to preventable diseases.
The order also recommended splitting the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering the shots at separate medical visits.
Kennedy had in January cut the US immunisation schedule to remove shots against six out of 17 diseases, a move halted by a federal court ruling.
The Trump order says that the federal government will now only support the remaining 11 shots.
The American Academy of Pediatrics and vaccine maker Merck criticised the order.
“We are evaluating our next steps," said Richard Hughes IV, lead counsel for the American Academy of Pediatrics, which sued earlier this year over Kennedy's changes to the childhood immunisation schedule.
Merck said there is no published scientific evidence showing any benefit to splitting the combination MMR shot into three, and that using the individual components increases the number of injections and can lead to delayed or missed immunisations.
"Effective immediately, my administration is recognising gold-standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up," Trump said during a White House signing ceremony.
Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the US National Center for Immunisation and Respiratory Diseases, said breaking up combination vaccines and downgrading recommendations would deepen disparities and worsen vaccine coverage, warning that the resulting recommendations in practice cannot be implemented.
Kennedy has previously led efforts to drop universal recommendations for hepatitis B shots for children and reduce the list of recommended vaccines, citing links to autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked. The executive order says it reaffirms Kennedy's overhaul despite the ongoing litigation.
Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician who chairs the Senate health committee, condemned the order.
"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that breaking up vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."
Cassidy, however, has shepherded Trump's slate of health agency leaders through confirmation despite his own warnings about vaccine scepticism. He cast a decisive vote to confirm Kennedy in 2025.
Cassidy lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-endorsed challenger and will leave office in January.
Trump, Kennedy and other White House officials said the order means US children would receive far fewer than the 72 injections recommended under the previous schedule.
Vaccine experts say that figure is inflated, because it counts combination shots such as MMR as multiple injections even though they are given in one shot, and assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses.
Dr Elizabeth Mack, a paediatric critical care physician in Charleston, South Carolina, said breaking up the shots would increase the number of injections children receive, because they are currently given in combination. She also said there were no licensed single-antigen measles, mumps or rubella vaccines available in the United States, making the recommendation unfeasible as written.
"We don't have a system that supports this," Mack said, questioning whether parents would be asked to make more visits and whether those visits would be reimbursed. (Reuters)
Edited by Cecil Wong

sources.news_title: Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine • Maine Morning Star
sources.text:
Trump urges shift in childhood vaccine recommendations, calls for splitting up MMR vaccine
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California. (Photo by Illustration Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Monday signed a sweeping executive order that aims to reshape guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, standing alongside Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and was met with immediate pushback.
The order — which calls on federal programs and funding to “support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines” — came as Trump continued to erroneously connect vaccines with autism during the White House event and his administration has sought to de-emphasize childhood vaccinations’ importance.
“This updated recommendation finally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world,” Trump said during a signing ceremony in the Oval Office, joined by Kennedy, a longtime opponent of vaccines, as well as National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya and “Make America Healthy Again” advocate Jayme Franklin, also founder and CEO of The Conservateur lifestyle brand, and others.
“More importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge,” Trump added.
What the order can legally accomplish was unclear as it’s up to states to decide which recommendations to follow.
GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, rebutted the new order on social media. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy said. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”
Splitting up MMR vaccine
The order recognizes “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” and divides the childhood immunization recommendations into three categories.
The order recommends all children receive immunizations for 11 diseases, including for “measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella.”
Immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations include: “respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue.”
The order also lists “hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza, and COVID-19” as immunizations “based on shared clinical decision-making.”
Trump’s executive order also calls for splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine into three separate single-disease shots and recommends that “all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.” Such single-disease shots are not currently available in the United States, White House officials acknowledged on a background call, but said they believe work will occur in the private sector to make that option eventually available.
“For example, at one year, you should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than getting them all in the same day,” Trump said during the signing ceremony.
Trump said the order also directs the attorney general “to advance legal challenges against states that violate children’s rights to religious or medical vaccination exemptions.”
‘Uncertainty and fear and confusion’
Meanwhile, Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, told reporters Monday during a press briefing after the Trump event that “the only thing that I can see is going to happen as a result of the announcement from today is an injection of greater amounts of uncertainty and fear and confusion, when there doesn’t need to be any of that.”
Many states rely on the AAP, rather than the federal government, for guidance surrounding childhood vaccines, according to the health research organization KFF, following earlier moves on vaccines during the Trump administration.
Rep. Frank Pallone, ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, blasted Trump’s order, saying the effort “lets political appointees attempt to overrule decades of peer-reviewed science and dictate vaccine schedules to American families,” in a statement.
The New Jersey Democrat added that “parents deserve accurate, trusted medical guidance, not a White House-curated list designed to rubberstamp Secretary Kennedy’s radical anti-vaccine agenda.”
Democrats from a coalition of states filed suit earlier this year over Trump administration changes to the federal vaccine guidelines, as did medical groups, but White House officials said Trump’s recommendations were not related to the litigation and were within his authority.

sources.news_title: Trump’s directive pushes for overhaul of school vaccine mandates
sources.text:
Many medical experts cast the push as scientifically baseless and potentially damaging to public health.
Curbing vaccines has been a key priority for health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit and has long promoted a disproven link between immunisation and autism.
The federal government does not have direct control over several areas covered by the order. States, for example, have the authority to require vaccinations for students to attend school.
On these points Trump’s move is more of a suggestion than an order.
“States and territories are advised to review” the Trump administration’s recommendations on “immunisation requirements for contexts such as school enrollment and attendance,” the order states.
In another section, it says the US health and human services department will form a task force to offer the MMR shot as individual vaccines “by working with the private sector and other countries as appropriate, while guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines and those vaccines recommended for shared clinical decision-making.”
New York City’s health commissioner, Alister Martin, said the order was based “in politics and conspiracy theories.”
“Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be,” Martin said in a statement.
“Cities and states can set their own recommendations and requirements, and many, including New York City, have moved away from the federal government’s recommendations as they’ve become politicised and unscientific.”
Years of clinical evidence support the safety of a combined MMR vaccine.
Public health experts have long advised that the combined shot offers children more protection faster, and also decreases the logistical hurdles for parents who may struggle to make multiple appointments.
Yet during the Oval Office signing, Trump made a series of incendiary and unsupported statements countering that advice.
In a call with reporters, Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), estimated it would take more than a decade to develop approved separated vaccines in the US.
“We’re advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data,” added Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.
Worst measles outbreak in decades
Senator Bill Cassidy, a doctor whose deciding vote confirmed Kennedy’s controversial appointment as health chief, posted on X that the president’s initiative would only serve to “increase hesitancy and make children less safe.”
“This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism,” Cassidy said.
The Trump administration’s push to overhaul vaccine policy comes as its efforts to implement major changes were blocked by a federal court earlier this year, pending further court proceedings.
The judge’s stay preventing the overhaul sided with major medical organizations, which asserted that the Trump administration’s actions to push the changes through were unlawful.
The president’s latest order arrives just as children across the country are readying to return to school, and as the US suffers its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.
Trump’s health secretary Kennedy is accused of contributing significantly to the crisis by spreading anti-vaccine sentiment and fueling fears of well-studied and proven immunisations.
Polling indicates that most Americans still support vaccination, and in recent months both Kennedy and Trump had backed off anti-vaccination rhetoric which could spell negative repercussions in November’s midterm vote.
But Monday’s efforts show the issue remains a core component of their health policy agenda, as both men remain committed to the false notion that vaccines can cause autism.
Such a potential link has been debunked by years of research.

sources.news_title: Trump Vaccines Executive Order: MMR Vaccine Schedule, Costs and Risks
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday that would substantially reshape federal childhood vaccine recommendations, narrowing the list of diseases for which vaccination is recommended for all children to 11 and calling for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to be divided into three separate shots. The trump vaccinesinitiative also directs the Department of Health and Human Services to review vaccine timing, sequencing, safety and alternative products.
The order, signed Aug. 10, does not simply eliminate vaccines. It establishes three categories: vaccines recommended for all children, vaccines recommended for certain high-risk groups and vaccines subject to shared clinical decision-making between patients, parents and clinicians. It also advises states to consider changing laws governing school vaccination requirements.
The move is one of the most consequential changes to U.S. childhood vaccine policy under Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. It also comes as the United States is experiencing a major resurgence of measles: the CDC reported 2,465 confirmed U.S. measles cases in 2026 through Aug. 6, compared with 2,289 for all of 2025.
What the Trump executive order on vaccines changes
The order identifies 11 diseases for which immunization is recommended for all children:
- measles
- mumps
- rubella
- diphtheria
- tetanus
- pertussis
- polio
- Haemophilus influenzae type B
- pneumococcal disease
- human papillomavirus
- varicella
This is an important distinction: the order refers to 11 diseases, not simply 11 vaccine injections or 11 vaccine products. Some vaccines protect against more than one disease.
The White House says the new framework represents a reduction from recommendations covering 18 diseases under the 2024 CDC schedule. The administration argues that the new approach is closer to vaccination practices in other developed countries and gives parents more flexibility.
Vaccines outside the 11-disease core are not banned.
The order places some immunizations into categories for high-risk populations or shared clinical decision-making. The White House text lists RSV monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal vaccines and dengue among high-risk recommendations, while also listing hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19 under shared clinical decision-making. The overlapping treatment of hepatitis A and hepatitis B is one detail that will require clarification during implementation.
The MMR vaccine schedule is the most controversial change
The executive order calls for the combined MMR vaccine schedule to be replaced, once possible, with three separate single-disease shots for measles, mumps and rubella.
It also says that, “to the maximum extent feasible,” childhood immunizations should be administered during separate medical visits.
The practical problem is immediate: standalone measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not currently licensed and available in the United States as separate products.
Reuters reported that no licensed single-antigen measles, mumps or rubella vaccines are currently available in the U.S. CBS likewise reported that Merck stopped making standalone versions in 2009 and that no company has announced a new U.S. product.
The order therefore does not mean that American pediatricians can begin giving children three separate MMR injections immediately.
Instead, it directs HHS to develop plans, including working with the private sector and other countries, to make single-vaccine options available while maintaining access to combination vaccines. The HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines has 90 days to present plans covering vaccine sequencing, alternative adjuvants, safety monitoring and other issues.
Does splitting MMR make vaccines safer?
The administration has argued that additional research is needed on vaccine safety and sequencing. Trump has repeatedly raised autism in discussions surrounding vaccines.
But the scientific evidence does not establish that MMR vaccination causes autism.
The AP reported that decades of research have found no link between vaccines and autism. Reuters also reported that the autism-vaccine connection promoted by Kennedy and Trump has been repeatedly debunked by scientists.
There is also no established evidence that separating MMR into individual vaccines provides a safety advantage.
Merck, which manufactures the combined MMR vaccine, said there is no published scientific evidence demonstrating a benefit from splitting the combination vaccine. The company and medical experts have warned that separate administration could increase the number of injections and create more opportunities for delayed or missed doses.
The order does direct HHS to conduct further safety research, including research into alternative adjuvants and continuous evaluation of vaccine risk-benefit profiles. That is a real component of the initiative and should be distinguished from the unsupported claim that existing evidence shows MMR causes autism.
Why medical groups oppose the Trump vaccine changes
The principal criticism is that the new policy could make childhood vaccination more complicated at precisely the time when U.S. vaccination coverage has weakened.
The American Academy of Pediatrics has opposed the administration’s changes. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a physician and chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, also criticized the executive order.
Cassidy argued that separating combination vaccines could result in children receiving more, rather than fewer, injections to obtain the same protection.
The concern is practical as much as scientific.
A child who receives multiple vaccines during one appointment can complete more of the recommended schedule without returning repeatedly to a doctor’s office. If vaccines are deliberately spread across separate appointments, parents may have to make additional trips, potentially creating more opportunities for missed appointments or delayed immunization.
The American College of Physicians warned that the changes could increase costs to patients and families, including additional copayments, while placing a greater logistical burden on families.
The financial consequences are still largely unknown
There is no comprehensive federal estimate of the financial cost of the executive order.
That is one of the most important unresolved issues.
The order requires HHS to develop new vaccine options, conduct additional research, improve safety monitoring and reassess the timing and sequencing of childhood vaccines. It says implementation is subject to applicable law and the availability of appropriations.
The potential costs fall into several categories.
More medical appointments
If vaccines are routinely administered at separate visits, pediatric practices could have to schedule more appointments to deliver the same number of immunizations.
That could increase administrative and staffing costs and create additional pressure on pediatric practices.
Families could also face higher out-of-pocket costs if additional visits generate copayments or other charges. The American College of Physicians has specifically warned about this possibility.
New vaccine manufacturing
Creating commercially available individual measles, mumps and rubella vaccines would require manufacturers to develop or restart production, obtain regulatory approval and establish distribution.
The executive order directs HHS to work with the private sector and other countries to develop these options, but it provides no public estimate of the cost or timeline.
Possible costs from preventable disease
The largest economic uncertainty is indirect.
If changes in recommendations lead to lower vaccination rates, the United States could face higher costs from outbreaks, medical treatment, hospitalizations, public-health investigations, school disruptions and lost work.
That is not a forecast that the executive order will necessarily produce those costs. It is a risk that will depend heavily on how vaccination coverage changes.
The CDC’s current data show why the issue matters. As of Aug. 6, 2026, the agency had recorded 2,465 confirmed measles cases and 38 outbreaks. Ninety-four percent of confirmed cases were associated with outbreaks.
The U.S. anti-vaccine movement: who supports it and what does the evidence show?
The measles problem makes the timing particularly significant
The policy arrives as U.S. measles vaccination coverage is already below the level generally considered necessary to maintain strong community protection.
CDC data show that MMR coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% during the 2019-20 school year to 92.5% in 2024-25. The CDC estimates that approximately 286,000 kindergartners were at risk during the 2024-25 school year.
Two doses of MMR are about 97% effective against measles, according to the CDC. One dose is about 93% effective.
That makes the administration’s argument and the critics’ argument fundamentally different.
The White House says reducing the number of routinely recommended vaccines and giving parents greater choice can improve trust and align U.S. recommendations with other developed nations.
Medical groups argue that reducing universal recommendations and making vaccination more cumbersome could lower coverage and increase the risk of preventable disease.
The available data cannot yet establish which outcome will occur.
Who are the most prominent supporters?
What does Trump expect the initiative to achieve?
The administration’s stated objective is to create what it calls “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations.”
The White House says the policy is intended to maximize parental choice, align U.S. recommendations with peer developed countries and improve vaccine research and safety monitoring.
The order also directs HHS to reassess the timing and sequencing of all core childhood vaccines and to conduct additional research into vaccine safety.
Which vaccines are most heavily criticized?
But the administration has not publicly established a numerical target for success.
It has not specified, for example, how much vaccination coverage should increase, how many adverse events it expects to prevent, how much money should be saved or what level of measles reduction would demonstrate that the policy worked.
That makes the policy difficult to evaluate against a defined baseline.
The order does not automatically change every state vaccine mandate
The executive order also has an important legal limitation.
States retain authority over many school-entry vaccination requirements. The White House is not simply replacing state vaccine laws with a federal rule.
Instead, the order advises states and territories to review their laws and consider aligning them with the new federal recommendations. It separately directs the Justice Department, Education Department and HHS to address federal and constitutional obligations concerning parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations and exemptions where applicable.
PBS also reported that states, rather than the federal government, have the authority to impose vaccination requirements for schoolchildren.
That means the practical effect of the order could vary significantly from state to state.
What does research actually say about vaccine risks?
What remains unanswered
Several major questions remain unresolved.
When will separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines become available?
The order calls for their development or availability, but there is currently no licensed U.S. supply of standalone products.
How much will the transition cost?
The administration has not released a comprehensive estimate covering federal spending, manufacturer investment, healthcare-provider costs or potential additional costs for families.
Who will pay for additional appointments?
The order calls for separate visits where feasible, but it does not establish a universal reimbursement mechanism for potentially additional medical encounters.
Will insurers change coverage?
The effect on private insurance, Medicaid and other payers remains to be determined through implementation and subsequent policy decisions.
Will vaccination rates rise or fall?
This is perhaps the most important empirical question. The administration expects greater flexibility to improve confidence, while medical groups warn that additional complexity could reduce vaccination coverage.
How will states respond?
States are only advised to review their school-entry requirements. The extent to which they adopt the federal framework is uncertain.
What will happen to vaccines moved out of the universal category?
The order does not prohibit those vaccines. Some remain available through high-risk recommendations or shared clinical decision-making. The practical implications for access, reimbursement and physician recommendations remain unclear.
What evidence will determine future changes?
The order gives the HHS Task Force 90 days to present plans and calls for continuing reassessment. The quality, transparency and independence of that research will be central to the next stage of the policy.
Why do vaccine-safety debates persist?
What happens next
The immediate next step is an HHS review of vaccine timing, sequencing, safety monitoring and the development of single-antigen vaccine options.
Within 90 days, the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines is directed to present plans to the president. Those plans are expected to address MMR and other core vaccines, alternative adjuvants, safety monitoring and additional research.
The order also leaves open the possibility of further changes to the federal childhood vaccine schedule.
For now, the biggest practical change is not that American children will immediately stop receiving vaccines. Rather, the Trump administration has established a new federal framework in which 11 diseases are designated for routine vaccination of all children, other immunizations are moved into more individualized categories, and the administration is pursuing a future system in which combination vaccines—including MMR—could be replaced or supplemented by individual shots.
Whether that produces lower costs and greater public confidence, as the administration argues, or lower vaccination coverage and higher disease risk, as critics warn, will depend on implementation and measurable changes in vaccination rates and disease incidence.
The first test will come as federal agencies, states, physicians, insurers and vaccine manufacturers determine how the new recommendations can actually be put into practice.
