sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations
Trump Signs Order Cutting Childhood Vaccines, Cites Autism
sources.text:
President Trump signed an executive order Monday calling for a reduced number of routine childhood vaccines, directing federal health officials to reassess the vaccine schedule within 90 days and repeatedly invoking autism as he did so, despite decades of scientific research that has found no causal link between vaccines and autism. The order has since drawn sharp, widening criticism from the medical establishment, with major professional organizations and at least one vaccine manufacturer disputing the scientific basis for the changes.
The order recommends children receive immunizations against 11 diseases, down from the 18 diseases the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended as of 2024, and organizes the vaccine schedule into new categories, with shots for diseases such as RSV and hepatitis A and B reserved for higher-risk children rather than universally recommended. It also calls for splitting the combined measles-mumps-rubella vaccine into three separate doses administered at separate visits, a change the administration frames as reducing the cumulative number of injections given to infants. "In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children," Trump said in the Oval Office as he signed the order, adding that spacing out vaccinations would result in nothing bad happening to children who follow the new schedule.
The American Medical Association's president said Monday that Trump's new recommendations put children's health at risk, joining what has become a broad chorus of medical criticism. Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, called the order not only disheartening but dangerous, warning on a call with reporters that spreading vaccinations out over additional medical visits could make it harder for parents to get their children fully immunized and could ultimately lower vaccination rates rather than improve safety. Merck, the pharmaceutical company that manufactures the combined MMR vaccine, said in a statement that its vaccine is supported by decades of clinical and real-world evidence, and warned that separating the shots into three doses may result in delayed or missed immunizations. Democratic Rep. Lauren Underwood, one of several physicians serving in Congress who criticized the order, said extensive evidence from decades of scientific studies shows no link between vaccines and autism and urged parents with questions to consult their child's physician rather than the new federal guidance.
Not all reaction was critical. Dr. Robert Redfield, who led the CDC during Trump's first term, praised the announcement, telling Fox News the order did not take away any vaccine from anyone but simply recommended that 11 vaccines serve as the standard regimen for American children. Heidi Overton, a White House public health policy adviser, said the order was a direct response to a federal judge's decision in March blocking an earlier CDC effort to narrow the recommended schedule, and that the administration intends to work directly with states to implement the changes rather than wait for the litigation to resolve, so that parents benefit from any resulting state-law changes immediately.
Trump tied the changes explicitly to autism throughout his remarks, saying the administration was working toward what he called the best vaccine recommendations in the entire world while acknowledging that the exact cause of autism remains unknown. The order itself does not name autism directly, but builds on a broader push by the administration and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine skeptic, to link the two; the CDC revised its own online vaccine guidance in November to suggest a possible connection, a change public health researchers characterized as a departure from established science. Large-scale studies conducted over more than two decades, including population-level research involving millions of children, have consistently found no causal relationship between vaccines and autism, a scientific consensus that predates and has not been altered by the administration's recent actions.
The order also directs the Justice Department to investigate whether states are complying with religious, medical and disability-related exemptions for childhood vaccine mandates, and signals the administration intends to press states to align their own requirements with the new federal recommendations, even though vaccine schedules and school entry requirements are set primarily at the state level. The move follows a January CDC recommendation, later blocked by a federal judge in March, to similarly reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccinations, and comes after the American Academy of Pediatrics broke publicly with the CDC to continue recommending the fuller 18-disease schedule.
The order drew swift criticism from within Trump's own party as well. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician who expressed hesitancy last year over confirming Kennedy to lead HHS specifically because of his vaccine and autism views, condemned the order on social media, writing that breaking up the combined MMR vaccine would mean children need more shots to achieve the same protection rather than fewer, and warning it would increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Republican lawmakers in Congress were largely silent in the immediate aftermath of the order, with Cassidy remaining the most prominent GOP voice publicly breaking with the administration's approach.
The order emerged from the administration's broader Make America Healthy Again initiative, which Trump established via executive order in February 2025 and tasked with investigating childhood chronic disease, later releasing a strategy document outlining more than 120 policy initiatives. A White House fact sheet framed Monday's order as reaffirming what it called gold standard science and empowering parents and doctors with maximum flexibility, noting that most peer nations maintain high childhood vaccination rates through public trust and education rather than government mandates, a characterization that omits the extent to which those countries' guidance continues to reflect the same vaccine-autism consensus the administration's order moves away from.
Whether states move to align their own school-entry vaccine requirements with the new federal recommendations, and whether the Justice Department's review of state-level exemptions leads to further legal action, are likely to determine how much practical effect Monday's order has beyond its immediate political and scientific controversy. Litigation is also a strong possibility, given that a similar CDC effort to narrow the recommended schedule was blocked in court earlier this year, and the widening rift between the administration and major medical organizations suggests the order's implementation is likely to remain contested well beyond the 90-day review period it sets in motion.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order to limit recommended childhood vaccines to 11
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump signed a new executive order regulating the vaccination calendar for children, which stipulates fewer shots by limiting the inoculation schedule to 11 immunizations, despite criticism.
The order also recommended splitting the childhood measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three shots and delivering the shots at separate medical visits.
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in January cut the U.S. immunization schedule to remove shots against six out of 17 diseases, a move halted by a federal court ruling. The Trump order says that the federal government will now only support the remaining 11 shots.
The American Academy of Pediatrics and vaccine maker Merck criticized the order.
Public health experts say the immunization schedule was based on decades of evidence showing that the vaccines could protect against serious illness and death, and that the number of shots reflects the specific health needs of Americans. They say reducing the recommended vaccines will leave more children vulnerable to preventable diseases.
"Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up," Trump said during a White House signing ceremony.
The U.S. ended in January its longstanding guidance that all children receive vaccines against flu and three other diseases, a sweeping change that advances one of Kennedy's long-term goals.
Kennedy, a longtime vaccine critic, has previously led efforts to drop universal recommendations for hepatitis B shots for children and reduce the list of recommended vaccines, citing links to autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.
The executive order says it reaffirms Kennedy's overhaul despite the ongoing litigation.

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order establishing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday establishing “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations” that would limit routine immunizations recommended for all children to protection against 11 diseases, aligning federal guidance more closely with practices in peer developed countries while maximizing parental choice and directing further research into safer options.
The order, titled “Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans,” formalizes three categories of childhood and adolescent immunizations based on a Health and Human Services Department scientific assessment. It changes the federal framework for vaccines recommended for all children, while placing other immunizations in categories for certain high-risk groups or shared clinical decision-making.
Immunizations recommended for all children under the new framework are those targeting measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella.
A second category covers immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY and dengue.
A third category consists of immunizations based on shared clinical decision-making between parents and clinicians: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19.
The order also states that the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should be administered as three separate single-disease shots once such products become domestically available, and that, to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be given at separate medical visits.
“For long and far too long, long period of time, America has recommended more childhood vaccines than any peer nation, and even twice as many doses as some European countries,” Trump said during the Oval Office signing ceremony. “In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children. […] Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing Gold Standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR. [..] We want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times.”
Trump linked the changes in part to concerns about rising autism rates, saying decades earlier children received far fewer vaccines and were healthier, with lower autism incidence.
“While we do not know exactly what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world,” he said. He described spreading doses across multiple visits over a year or longer so children receive a smaller fraction of shots at once.
The White House noted that an HHS scientific assessment found the United States currently recommends more childhood vaccines than any peer nation, including more than twice as many doses as some European countries. In 1980, children following the CDC schedule received 23 doses in seven shots against seven diseases.
By 2024 that had risen to at least 84 doses in at least 57 shots for 17 diseases, plus RSV monoclonal antibody protection, for a total of 18. The assessment identified a consensus set of vaccines consistently recommended across peer nations and found most of those nations maintain high vaccination rates through public trust and education rather than mandates.
The order advises states and territories to review the recommendations and consider updating immunization requirements for school enrollment based on the assessment and peer-country practices. It directs all executive departments and agencies to advance the recommendations to the fullest extent allowed by law.
To maximize parental choice, the attorney general is instructed to support meritorious legal actions challenging state laws that conflict with constitutional and federal statutory obligations regarding parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations and equal protection, including requirements to provide religious and medical exemptions. The Departments of Justice, Education and Health and Human Services must ensure their contractors and grantees comply with those obligations.
The secretary of Health and Human Services, through the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, is directed to present plans to the president within 90 days. Those plans are to include options for administering core vaccines, beginning with MMR, as single rather than combination products while preserving access to combinations, assessing ideal timing and sequencing, developing additional alternative adjuvants to aluminum and conducting comparative safety and efficacy studies, ensuring continuous evaluation of risk-benefit profiles using U.S. and international data, and improving safety monitoring, transparency and research.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the administration “will preserve access to vaccines, strengthen safety monitoring, expand research, give doctors and parents better information, and restore informed consent and parental choice to their rightful place in American medicine.”
National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya said the order “restores the autonomy of families and parents to make good decisions for their kids” while continuing to emphasize science and restoring “a healthy relationship between public health and parents.”
White House Domestic Policy Council Deputy Director Heidi Overton noted the order encourages willing states to incorporate the recommendations into law so parents enrolling children in school would not face requirements for vaccines no longer recommended for all children, bringing U.S. practice more in line with European nations.
The order builds on a December 2025 presidential memorandum directing alignment of core childhood vaccine recommendations with peer-country best practices, a subsequent HHS scientific assessment, and a May 2026 executive order. Implementation of earlier steps had been delayed by litigation over the composition of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and related updates.
The new order reaffirms that federal programs and funding should support maximal parental choice consistent with constitutional and statutory obligations, personal autonomy and informed consent, while preserving access to currently available vaccines.

sources.news_title: Child vaccine schedule reduced as Trump moves to dramatically shift medical power to parents
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is spearheading a major overhaul of current childhood vaccination mandates in an effort to give parents more freedom to choose which shots their children take, and when.
Trump signed an Executive Order announcing what the administration is calling the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations, saying that not only do the new recommendations align with other developed nations, but they also with common sense.
A memo on the order recommends children receive immunizations for 11 diseases, fewer than the 18 current Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines. It also ended recommendations that all minors receive the COVID-19 jab.
A Health and Human Services (HHS) scientific assessment compared the U.S. vaccine schedule to those of peer nations in Europe. It found that the American childhood vaccine schedule recommends many more vaccines than most western nation counterparts — sometimes close to double the number of shots.
SWITZERLAND FIRES HOCKEY COACH WHO ADMITTED TO FAKING VACCINATION STATUS FOR 2022 BEIJING OLYMPICS
The memo recommends that parents should have five separate vaccine appointments, instead of children taking all of the vaccines at once.
"I think you're going to see some amazing results [by] breaking it up," Trump said in the Oval Office while announcing the order on Monday.
"It's not just that you're doing fewer vaccines or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor. Much smaller amounts."
Trump has previously voiced opposition to appointments where babies and toddlers are given multiple vaccinations at one time.
The memo on Trump's latest health-related executive action stresses flexibility for parents, urging them to "make individualized decisions for higher-risk children through shared clinical decision-making."
The memo also recommends separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines into separate shots, instead of taking all three vaccines at once, as is common. It also notes that the U.S. is in the minority of peer nations that mandates vaccinations in order for children to enroll in school.
Additionally, the order focuses on discriminatory practices based on vaccine status.
"In addition, this executive order directs the Attorney General to advance legal challenges against states that violate children's rights to religious or medical vaccination exemptions," Trump said.
"Parents can still choose to give their children all of the vaccinations if they wish, it's up to the parents — we're making recommendations that are strong – but it's up to the parents if they wish and they will be covered by insurance," he continued. "However, this updated recommendation finally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world. More importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge."
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
The order is part of Trump's commitment to Make America Healthy Again (MAHA). Last year, the president, by executive order, launched the MAHA Commission, aimed at addressing the causes of what the administration says is an "escalating" health crises.
The commission was specifically directed to investigate childhood chronic diseases. The probe led to "a sweeping plan with more than 120 initiatives to reverse the failed policies that fueled America’s childhood chronic disease epidemic."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The White House did not provide further comment when reached about the latest initiative.

sources.news_title: Trump order recommends breaking up MMR vaccine into 3 doses
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order recommending that the childhood MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella, be split into three vaccines administered at three separate doctor visits.
In addition to the changes to the MMR vaccine, Trump’s order also directs U.S. health officials to improve vaccine research, according to The Associated Press.
Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™
Point phone camera here
During his signing ceremony, Trump said “nothing bad can happen” with his move. But public health experts have raised concerns about separating vaccine routines. They suggest that it could lead to an increased risk of children becoming infected with vaccine-preventable diseases between doctor visits. There are currently no separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the U.S.
Trump’s order comes at a time when measles cases are rising in the U.S. On Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed that the country has seen nearly 2,500 cases of the disease since the year began. That’s already more than all the cases seen in 2025, according to CDC data. According to a letter published in May in The Lancet, the U.S. is “highly likely” to lose its measles elimination status this November.
Trump, along with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has tried to connect childhood vaccines with the increasingly prevalent number of autism in children. The president has increased pressure on Kennedy to identify the cause of autism, something that Kennedy had hoped to do with new research he unveiled last year. In September, the administration claimed that the over-the-counter medication Tylenol was linked to autism. But previous, large-scale studies about the drug found no link.
Vaccines are rigorously studied. To date, no credible study has ever definitively linked vaccines to autism.
Changes to vaccine guidelines
When it comes to schools, the federal government has little say in what schoolchildren are required to have before they start class. States, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for students.
The order will advise states with school vaccine requirements to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration’s new recommendations, according to the order.
In December, Trump ordered HHS to review how other nations implement their vaccine guidelines and to consider revisions to U.S. guidance. In response, the department cut the number of vaccines it recommends for children, but that move has since been blocked in court. Health experts said at the time of the decision that it was based on incomplete scientific evidence.
The lack of evidence and studies pointing to their conclusion that vaccines may cause autism hasn’t stopped the administration. On Monday, Kennedy again said that he believes an unknown environmental factor is the cause of rising autism diagnoses. He said his department will release the evidence they have found “as soon as they are ready,” the AP reported.
It is true that autism diagnoses have dramatically risen over the last few decades. The CDC’s Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network, which estimates how many children meet the criteria for autism spectrum disorder every two years, found that the prevalence of autism among 8-year-olds has risen nearly fivefold in the past two decades.
But researchers don’t point to vaccines as the reason. Instead, they say that increased awareness of the disorder could explain some of the rise. But others say that it could be because of other factors like the maternal age being higher than it was in the past, or even maternal obesity rates.

sources.news_title: The Latest: Trump signs executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that certain shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits. The order will recommend separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots administered in separate visits, and direct the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research. Even as the order calls for revised vaccine recommendations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
Trump swore in Todd Blanche, his old personal lawyer, as attorney general Monday. Meanwhile, Iran says it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States lifts its blockade on the strait, pays compensation for months of war damage, lifts economic sanctions and releases Iran’s frozen assets. And Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu flatly rejected Trump's proposed exit strategy for Gaza.
Here’s the latest:
Trump spokesperson suggests separating MMR vaccine could help instill trust in the vaccines
White House spokesperson Kush Desai said Monday that Trump’s call for the development of separate, single-disease measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for U.S. children will help generate trust in vaccine hesitant parents.
“President Trump is one of countless parents who have voiced questions and concerns about the combined MMR vaccine,” Desai told The Associated Press, saying the separate vaccines will “give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children, which ultimately will increase vaccination rates for all three diseases.”
The White House didn’t provide new scientific evidence supporting the move. Studies of babies and toddlers in the U.S. have shown that the use of combination shots increased the likelihood of completing all recommended vaccinations by the age of 2.
Pediatricians say executive order spreads confusion about vaccines, which are safe
Doctors from the American Academy of Pediatrics said the executive order spreads uncertainty and confusion.
Dr. Aaron Milstone, pediatric director of infection prevention at Johns Hopkins Health System, said doctors want to reassure parents there are “many, many, many years of scientific data highlighting the safety of vaccines in children.”
The timing of vaccines has also been well-studied, he said.
“We give vaccines to children even when they’re young because we know that’s safe and because we know it’s the best time for their body to respond to that vaccine in a good way and to make their body stronger to fight off an infection if they’re exposed to that,” Milstone said.
The potential link between vaccines and autism has also been studied exhaustively — in more than 40 well-designed studies in more than seven countries involving over five million children, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of American Academy of Pediatrics.
“I’m not sure that there is anything that has been as thoroughly looked at as this question about whether or not there is a link between autism and vaccines,” he said. “And the answer is unequivocally no.”
Republican senator blasts Trump executive order on vaccines
Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican, is strongly rebuking Trump’s executive order on vaccines.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy said in a social media post on X. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”
Cassidy chairs the Senate committee with oversight responsibilities for healthcare agencies. He went on to say that children will have to get more shots to get the same protection. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.
“Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy said.
Trump did not provide new evidence of a claimed link between vaccines and autism
The National Institutes of Health started funding research teams over a year ago charged with unearthing the cause autism, a portion of them assessing vaccines’ claimed role.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between childhood vaccines and autism.
Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the head of the institute, spoke at Trump’s executive order signing and said that “science takes time” and “you don’t get answers immediately.”
Still, Bhattacharya was more tentative about claiming an evidence-based link between autism and vaccines, generally avoiding the suggestion altogether.
“What we’ve done in this administration,” he said, “is we’ve given permission to scientists to honestly answer this question, to find the link for the first time.”
12 medical groups previously endorsed the childhood influenza vaccine. Trump’s executive order did not
In January, the American Academy of Pediatrics put out their 2026 childhood vaccine guidance, which included a jab for influenza, that got the green light from groups including the National Medical Association and Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society.
The AAP said in a press release at the time that over 80% of childhood deaths related to influenza were with unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated patients, adding that children under 5 years old are particularly vulnerable.
Trump said the vaccine is “no longer recommended for all children.”
Trump says Iran can still cause trouble but argues that it’s feeling financial squeeze
The president was dismissive of Iranian officials’ demands after Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei stressed that Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the U.S. meets its conditions, including paying reparations for the five-month-old war.
Trump during an Oval Office exchange with reporters claimed that the U.S. has “100% control” of the strait, but that the situation remains complex. He made the case that the U.S. Navy’s blockade of the strait is preventing Iran from selling its oil on the international market, a move that is effectively choking the Iranian economy.
“Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble, but they’re broke,” Trump said. “They have no money. You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And they’re not paying their soldiers.”
With measles raging, vaccine proponent said it’s no time for an ‘anti-vaccine agenda’
At a time when the U.S. is facing its worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years, “we should be making it easier to protect children from preventable disease, not harder,” said Northe Saunders, president of American Families for Vaccines.
He said “RFK’s anti-vaccine agenda” shouldn’t pressure state leaders to abandon protections that work for their communities.
“States have long played a central role in setting school immunization requirements,” he said. “and parents, educators, healthcare professionals, and state leaders should be able to make decisions about protecting children without political interference from the federal government.”
In late July, the number of measles cases in the U.S. has surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has logged more than 2,318 cases of measles this year.
Trump’s childhood vaccine recommendations contradict medical establishment
The president, at an executive order signing on new childhood vaccine recommendations, said that, “very importantly,” jabs for hepatitis B, COVID-19 and influenza “are no longer recommended for all children.”
Those vaccinations, however, are still recommended by the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics, among other medical groups.
While the latter organization recommends childhood vaccines for 18 diseases, Trump’s executive order limits that to prioritizing just 11.
Public health officials have raised concerns over some of Trump’s recommendations
That includes the presidents recommendation announced Monday to space out childhood vaccine shots instead of getting all of them on the same visit.
Public health officials say that could lead to children becoming infected with a vaccine-preventable disease in the periods between jabs.
Doctor urges parents to listen to medical experts about shots
Michael Osterholm, executive director of the Vaccine Integrity Project, said parents should continue to rely on vaccine recommendations developed by trusted medical and public health experts, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, when making decisions on shots for their kids.
“Today’s Executive Order does not change the underlying scientific evidence supporting childhood immunization. That data has been built over decades — through large clinical trials, real-world effectiveness studies and continuous safety monitoring involving millions of children,” he said in a statement.
“Parents deserve clear, evidence-based guidance about how to protect their children, not competing recommendations issued through political processes. When families receive conflicting messages, confidence in vaccination suffers, and children ultimately bear the consequences.”
Trump overstates dangers of vaccines
In announcing his executive order on vaccines, President Donald Trump said “bad things happen” when children get the combined MMR vaccine.
“I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination that looks like the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body, and bad things happen in, many cases-in too many cases,” he said.
But experts say the risk of serious side effects is extremely low and years of real-world data proves the vaccine is safe and effective. Common side effects include soreness and a mild rash or redness at the injection site, a fever, and temporary pain or stiffness in the joints.
Decades of studies have concluded there’s no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
Decades of autism research have found no single cause
Besides genetics, scientists have identified various possible factors, including the age of a child’s father, the mother’s weight, and whether she had diabetes or was exposed to certain chemicals.
Any concern that vaccines could be linked to autism has been long debunked, according to scientists and leading advocacy groups for people with autism.
Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Trump proposes new childhood vaccine recommendations, though power in schools rests with states
Trump, who suggested connections between autism and vaccines despite a scientific consensus that there isn’t a link, issued new guidance for childhood vaccines that space out shots and limit the number of recommended routine jabs.
Still, the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren rests with state governments.
Trump to sign executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots
President Donald Trump on Monday will sign an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits, according to a White House fact sheet.
The order will recommend administering each vaccine in its own visit and separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots and direct the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research, says the fact sheet, first reported by The Daily Caller. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for children are not available in the U.S.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
CBO says this year’s deficit will be larger than previously predicted, mostly because of smaller-than-expected tariff revenue
The Congressional Budget Office is projecting that this fiscal year’s deficit will be $2.1 trillion, about $200 billion more than what it predicted in early February.
The major reason for the change has to do with less revenue coming into the Treasury than projected as a result of the Supreme Court finding that the tariffs President Donald Trump imposed under an emergency powers law were unconstitutional.
The fiscal year runs through September 30.
Revenue totaled $4.5 trillion through the first 10 months of the fiscal year. That’s about 3% more than during the same period a year ago.
Meanwhile, spending increased about 5% from last year, rising to $6.3 trillion. Spending in the federal government’s major healthcare programs, Medicare and Medicaid, each increased by about 8%.
Trump signs waiver letting foreign trips carry oil and other goods among US ports for 90 days
Trump on Monday extended a waiver for 90 days for foreign ships to transport goods, including oil, fertilizers and other fossil fuel products, among U.S. ports.
The president first waived the Jones Act on March 17 so that it would be easier to transport oil and refined fuels among ports, reducing price pressures after the start of the war with Iran.
The extension will take effect on August 17.
Unlike previous extensions, the Pentagon will consult with the Maritime Administration to decide which voyages are exempt from the 1920 law containing the Jones Act. The waiver will only apply to cargo are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture and food, such as soybean oil.
Ex Air Force secretary talking to lawyers after Trump admin revokes security clearance
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall said Monday that he’s talking to lawyers after the Trump administration revoked his security clearance last week.
Kendall, who has been critical of the administration, said in a post on LinkedIn that he’s “talking to lawyers and will have more soon.” He said he’s had his clearance for 60 years and was careful to say nothing classified.
The Pentagon revoked Kendall’s “eligibility” to access classified information and barred him from holding “any sensitive position,” alleging Friday that he disclosed sensitive information about Air Force One’s capabilities to the media.
It follows reporting last month, including from The New York Times, on security concerns over the new, Qatari-gifted Air Force One, including that it lacked the advanced antimissile capabilities of its predecessor.
US military base in South Carolina renamed after late Sen. Lindsey Graham
A U.S. military base in South Carolina was renamed after the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham Monday, with Defense Department Sec. Pete Hegseth praising Graham’s dedication to the military and for “taking on a radical leftist ideology” in the armed forces.
Joint Base Charleston is now Joint Base Lindsey Graham, which includes an Air Force base and a Naval Weapons Station. Graham, who died last month, served in the Air Force, Air National Guard and reserves.
Hegseth praised Graham’s support of President Donald Trump’s historic $1.5 billion defense budget proposal. In praising Graham, Hegseth also employed the Trump administration’s strategy of linking Democrats to communism.
“The hard left declared war on our own military,” Hegseth said, adding that “it seems that many people have forgotten the reality of what communism looks like.”
Trump dismisses Iran’s call for war reparations
Trump is scoffing at the Iran’s call for reparations for devastation caused to the country by the U.S. and Israeli bombardment over the last five months, a demand he said hadn’t been raised by Tehran’s negotiators until now.
The Republican president, in a social media post, added that in response to the Iranian demand he’s directing negotiators to include “compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts.”
The U.S. government says Iran-backed militants have been responsible for the deaths and injuries of hundreds of Americans over the last several decades, including the 1983 bombing on a Marine compound in Beirut that killed 241 U.S. military personnel, the 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. Air Force housing complex in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. troops and wounded hundreds more, and the deaths of at least 603 U.S. troops in Iraq between 2003 and 2011.
Trump announces staff secretary Will Scharf will be his new White House counsel
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that his new White House counsel will be Will Scharf, the staff secretary who as the Trump-appointed head of the National Capital Planning Commission helped secure approval for the $400 million ballroom project.
Trump said that, beginning Sept. 1, Scharf will be replacing David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the Supreme Court.
“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”
The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture — just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican Party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.
Trump officials propose new scrutiny of food additives and ingredients
U.S. health officials on Monday proposed a rule change that would require food manufacturers to notify regulators before introducing new ingredients or additives into processed or packaged foods.
The proposal would change a decades-old policy that advocates have called a regulatory loophole, blaming it for allowing thousands of unvetted ingredients into the U.S. food supply.
Under the proposed rule from the Food and Drug Administration, companies would have to document and submit their safety findings for new ingredients, giving regulators the opportunity to investigate if they see a potential safety risk. Currently companies can decide for themselves if an ingredient or additive is “generally recognized as safe” and there is no requirement for companies to notify or submit evidence to the FDA, although some do.
State Department says it has revoked more 175,000 visas since Trump took office
The revoked visas had been granted to more than 175,000 foreigners who have endangered American citizens, broken laws or threatened U.S. national security, according to a statement issued Monday by the State Department.
The statement says most were revoked “due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity,” including assault, child abuse, drunken driving, drug violations, and embezzlement. It doesn’t say how many of those visa holders had been convicted of such crimes.
Some of the revocations involved “foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk, including one who stated ‘when fascists die, democrats don’t complain’ and another who said he ‘died too late’, the statement said.
Veteran Democrats face strong challenges in Connecticut’s primary
Democratic Gov. Ned Lamont’s try for a third term must first clear a challenge by state Rep. Josh Elliott. And U.S. Rep. John Larson faces his first primary challenge in nearly 30 years, from former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune and state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest.
Both contests could help redefine the Democratic brand by replacing old guard figures with younger alternatives. Tuesday’s primaries also could extend a progressive winning streak in New York City, Colorado and the Michigan U.S. Senate primary.
Larson turned 78 in July. Concerns over his health and age arose last year after he suffered a seizure while delivering a speech on the House floor.

sources.news_title: Trump signs order on childhood vaccination recommendations, citing autism
sources.text:
Trump signs order on childhood vaccination recommendations, citing autism
Washington (CBS NEWS) – Sources from CBS say President Trump signed an executive order on Monday laying out new recommendations for childhood vaccinations, saying that while “we do not know” exactly what the cause of autism is, it is “essential” to have the “best vaccine recommendations in the entire world.”
The executive order, obtained by CBS News before the president signed it, said there should be a more limited number of vaccines recommended for children. It directed the Health and Human Services Department to reassess vaccine sequencing and timing within 90 days. The executive order didn’t mention autism, but the president did — repeatedly.
“Today, we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s Gold Standard Childhood Vaccination Recommendations and that has to do with many subjects but including autism in particular,” the president said in the Oval Office with the executive order in front of him.
“Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today,” the president said. “In those times, people were much healthier and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So, there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism. And we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was.”
“While we do not know exactly what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world,” he continued. “So we’re reducing them, we’re changing it to visits over the period of a year, a year and a half, so they get 20% of what they would have gotten in one big shot.”
The president cited no evidence for his claims.
Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing. Research shows that genetics play a role in autism diagnoses. The NIH says some possible risk factors for autism include prenatal exposure to pesticides or air pollution, extreme prematurity or low birth weight, certain maternal health conditions, or parents conceiving at an older age.
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., said next month, the federal government’s Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health is “preparing a major new initiative focused on foundational causes and biology of autism.”
“We will examine every biologically plausible hypothesis and leave no legitimate, scientific question unexplored,” Kennedy said. “Mr. President, you have told us you want answers, so do I. We have just over two years to finish the work and I know you’re impatient. And we are moving with an urgency that that deadline demands. We will bring you actions and findings as soon as they are read.”
Mr. Trump promised “nothing bad can happen” from the research his administration is doing on autism.
CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Celine Gounder noted that studies have failed to show a link between autism and vaccines. A 2019 Danish study followed 657,461 children and found the autism rate in vaccinated kids was slightly lower. And a 2015 study of 95,727 American children included nearly 2,000 who had an older sibling with autism. If a vaccine had triggered autism in a genetically vulnerable child, links would have appeared, but their risk was no higher. The study found the MMR vaccine does not increase a child’s risk of autism.
The president called the announcement a “major victory” for parents and constitutional rights.
While the CDC advises states on policy, states set policies for school immunization schedules.
The draft order also encouraged single-dose vaccines, rather than combination shots, saying, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.” For instance, it recommends breaking the MMR vaccine into three shots. The order puts some vaccines, like RSV and hepatitis A and B, in a category of shots only for high-risk children.
This would upend decades of federal guidance on which vaccines are administered to children, just as the school year is about to begin in many states.
It comes after the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in January recommended reducing the number of childhood vaccinations, to cover 11 diseases. The American Academy of Pediatrics broke with the CDC and continued to recommend vaccination against 18 childhood diseases.
In March, a federal judge blocked the CDC’s recommended changes to the childhood vaccine schedule.
The order cited recent efforts to align the vaccine schedule with what it calls “best practices” from peer nations, along with protecting religious liberty and parental authority. But it acknowledges that litigation has resulted in delayed implementation of that push, leading the administration to pursue additional measures.
“In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children,” the president said.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a doctor, blasted the president’s executive order on X.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” he said. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong.”
The American Academy of Pediatrics pointed out tat so-called “peer nations” have different vaccination needs, and best practices vary. It said vaccine guidance may differ across countries because they face threats from different diseases, population demographics, health care systems and vaccine availability.
Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, was asked about plans for the executive order Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan.”
“I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it’s very important that parents vaccinate their kids,” Bhattacharya said.
“I trust the science” on childhood vaccines, Bhattacharya added, and noted that he has vaccinated his own children.
The executive order comes as measles cases have risen to their highest levels in 35 years. Bhattacharya, who’s also been serving as acting CDC director in recent months, acknowledged that the U.S. may lose its measles elimination status, while pointing to other countries that have recently lost their status.

sources.news_title: New Trump vaccine order targets MMR shot
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Monday signed a sweeping executive order establishing new “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” a policy that restructures which vaccines the federal government recommends for children and how they should be administered. The move accelerates the administration’s push to realign U.S. vaccine guidance with what it calls “best practices” from peer nations, while reviving a politically charged debate over childhood immunization ahead of the midterms.
Families, pediatricians and state health systems could soon face new rules, more appointments and shifting requirements as federal agencies reassess the entire childhood vaccine schedule.
The order declares that the United States currently recommends more childhood vaccines than any peer nation and directs the Department of Health and Human Services to reevaluate vaccine timing, sequencing and product options within 90 days. It also states that the combined MMR vaccine should be split into three single‑disease shots once available domestically and that “to the maximum extent feasible,” all childhood vaccines should be administered at separate medical visits.
As he prepared to sign it, Trump said the recommendations relate to “many subjects but including autism in particular,” despite the order itself not referencing autism.
What Is the MMR Vaccine?
The MMR vaccine is a long‑standing cornerstone of childhood immunization, designed to protect against measles, mumps and rubella—three highly contagious viral infections that can cause severe complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, blindness, hearing loss and, in rare cases, death.
For more than 60 years, the combined shot has dramatically reduced the circulation of these diseases in the United States, becoming one of the most effective tools in modern public health.
The vaccine contains weakened live viruses that train the immune system to recognize and fight off infection. According to the Cleveland Clinic, two doses are 97 percent effective at preventing measles and rubella and 86 percent effective at preventing mumps.
Children typically receive one dose between 12–15 months and a second between ages 4–6, though additional doses may be recommended during mumps outbreaks or for adults with uncertain vaccination histories.
What Is Trump’s New Infant Vaccine Schedule?
The executive order establishes a new federal framework that divides childhood immunizations into three categories: vaccines recommended for all children, vaccines recommended only for high‑risk groups, and vaccines offered through shared clinical decision‑making.
Under this structure, vaccines such as RSV monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A and B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY and dengue are moved into the high‑risk category, narrowing routine access.
The order also directs HHS to reassess the “ideal timing and sequencing” of all core childhood vaccines and adjust the federal schedule based on what it calls “gold‑standard science.”
Within 90 days, the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines must present plans to expand single‑disease vaccine options—starting with MMR—and evaluate alternative adjuvants, comparative safety data and improved monitoring systems.
The administration says these steps are intended to align U.S. recommendations with peer nations while preserving parental choice.
What Changes Under Trump’s New Pediatric Vaccine Policy?
One of the most significant changes is the directive that the combined MMR vaccine be administered as three separate shots once manufacturers can produce them domestically.
The order further states that “to the maximum extent feasible,” all childhood vaccines should be given at separate medical visits, a shift that would require families to schedule more appointments and pediatric practices to overhaul long‑standing workflows.
The order also encourages states and territories to review their school‑entry immunization laws and consider updating them in light of the new federal recommendations. It emphasizes parental authority, religious liberty and informed consent, and instructs the Department of Justice to support legal challenges to state laws that conflict with those principles.
These provisions revive earlier administration efforts to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines—efforts that courts froze earlier this year—and attempt to bypass those delays through executive action.
Pediatric Experts Warn Splitting MMR Shots Leaves Children Exposed Longer
Dr. Melissa Stockwell, Division Chief of Child and Adolescent Health at Columbia University and a pediatrician at NewYork‑Presbyterian Hospital, told Newsweek that there is “no scientific or public health rationale for splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots,” warning that the change “adds unnecessary extra burden for families” and “raises the risk of missed and delayed doses, leaving the child unprotected for longer.”
She stressed that measles, mumps and rubella “are not benign childhood illnesses,” noting that measles can cause “pneumonia and encephalitis,” mumps can lead to “hearing loss and reproductive complications,” and rubella poses “particular risk during pregnancy.”
Stockwell added that the combined MMR shot “has been extensively studied and used for decades” and that “there is no established clinical or immunologic benefit to separating out the MMR vaccine.”
Stockwell also pushed back on claims that children are being overloaded with vaccines. “The volume of immunizations children receive is actually quite small,” she said. “Using current combination vaccines, the total volume of routine early childhood immunizations is about two teaspoons.”
Even across all childhood and adolescent vaccines, she said, “the total amount is still only one tablespoon.” She added that the immune system encounters far more antigen during common infections: “One single bacterium can contain thousands of these antigens.”
She warned that delaying or spacing out vaccines “unnecessarily increases the time a child is most at risk,” especially amid “the largest resurgence of measles in decades.” Many families, she said, will be “more confused than ever” if the schedule requires extra visits, which would “place a significant burden on families” and strain pediatric practices.
Patsy Stinchfield, MS, PNP, Executive Director of the Measles Collaborative, said the MMR vaccine has been safely administered as a combined shot since 1971 and remains “a live combination vaccine that prevents measles, mumps, and rubella—all serious infectious diseases.”
She told Newsweek that single‑antigen measles vaccine “is not available in the U.S., and there is likely little incentive for a manufacturer to make one.”
“The vaccine works well,” she said. “More than 99% of people who receive two doses after their first birthday develop protective antibodies that are generally considered to provide lifelong immunity.” Mild fever or rash can occur in some children, she said, and febrile seizures are “very rare,” occurring in about “1 in 3,000 to 4,000 children.”
Stinchfield said splitting the MMR shot “is not an evidence‑based recommendation” and “makes no difference to the immune system—it recognizes the individual or the three together the same.”
But dividing the doses, she warned, “creates additional risks and burdens for families,” including more clinic visits, more needle pokes, higher costs and added strain on pediatric practices.
“With a national measles outbreak that has reached nearly 2,500 cases—more than all of 2025—we should be doing everything possible to increase vaccination uptake, not decrease it,” she said. “It is difficult to imagine a parent, clinician, or public health expert supporting a recommendation to divide the MMR vaccine into three separate shots and visits.”
Public Health Groups Say Order Is 'Not Grounded in New Evidence'
The Partnership to Fight Infectious Disease (PFID) said the executive order is “not anchored to an actual problem,” noting that “there have been no new safety signals, no new clinical findings, no reduced risk from vaccine‑preventable disease that would justify rewriting vaccine recommendations for America’s children.”
PFID said the ongoing measles outbreak — the worst in more than 30 years — shows the consequences of misinformation lowering vaccination rates.
“Repeating false and misleading information about the recommended childhood vaccine schedule, vaccine ingredients, and the safety and effectiveness of recommended vaccines does not make our children healthier or safer,” the group said. “It will only leave more American children vulnerable to preventable illness.”
The group warned that recommending multiple appointments “will only add to the strain on American families,” including time off work, added costs and greater exposure to illness in crowded waiting rooms.
“Families deserve consistency and clear, evidence‑based guidance,” PFID said. “They get that from family physicians, nurses, and pharmacists in their community.”
Sen. Bill Cassidy Condemns Trump’s Vaccine Order
Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican and physician, sharply criticized Trump’s executive order, arguing that splitting the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines into three separate appointments would undermine children’s safety rather than improve it.
In a post on X, Cassidy said the president “does not have the expertise to make these changes,” stressing that childhood vaccines are safe, effective and not linked to autism. He warned that requiring additional visits for the same level of protection would heighten hesitancy and leave children exposed to preventable diseases for longer.
Cassidy’s objections come as the administration continues its broader effort to reduce the number of routine childhood vaccines — a push that began with a January HHS proposal later halted by a federal judge.
The senator has repeatedly clashed with the administration over vaccine policy, including during the confirmation process for Erica Schwartz to lead the CDC, when he pressed her on whether she could shield the agency from political interference. Although he ultimately supported her nomination, Cassidy has remained vocal about what he sees as persistent pressure on federal health agencies.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Sam Wilson.

sources.news_title: President Trump signs executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots
sources.text:
NEW YORK — President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order recommends separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots administered in separate visits, and directs the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research, says a White House fact sheet, first reported by The Daily Caller. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for children are not currently available in the United States.
Speaking about the order at the Oval Office on Monday, Trump also said that one-year-olds should have their shots separated out into five separate visits, though it wasn’t clear whether he was talking about all the vaccines they receive or specific ones.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Even as the order calls for revised vaccine recommendations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren. The order will advise states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration’s recommendations, the fact sheet said.
Last December, Trump ordered HHS to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising U.S. guidance accordingly. The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, a move that has since been blocked in court.
In the months leading up to Monday’s announcement, Trump’s administration had largely pivoted away from talking about vaccine policy in favor of less polarizing topics like healthy eating and efforts to lower drug prices ahead of November’s elections. Polls show most Americans still support school vaccine requirements, though Republicans are less likely than Democrats to see them as important.
Still, Trump has been fixated on connecting autism to vaccines. He has recently ramped up pressure on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to identify the cause of autism, something Kennedy had pledged to do with new research unveiled last year. Trump publicly prodded the health secretary for an update on autism research in a Cabinet meeting last month.
“How are you doing on the autism research?” Trump asked.
“We will have an answer for you,” Kennedy said.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between childhood vaccines and autism. On Monday, Kennedy repeated his assertion that he believes an unknown environmental factor is to blame for rising autism diagnoses and said that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
Monday’s order comes as school years are starting around the country and the nation contends with a measles outbreak that experts say could result in the U.S. losing its measles elimination status.

sources.news_title: Trump order seeks to stagger childhood vaccination administration
sources.text:
Trump order seeks to stagger childhood vaccination administration
Cassidy, health groups decry move
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday to drastically change the childhood vaccine schedule by recommending shots be administered in separate visits to the doctor’s office.
The executive order acts on Trump’s long-held belief that splitting up routine childhood vaccinations across multiple visits lessens the risk of acquiring autism. Scientists have found no credible risk between vaccinations and autism.
“I’ve seen vaccinations the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body. And bad things happen,” Trump said at the Oval Office signing on Monday, where he thanked Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and “the MAHA moms.”
Trump said that, for instance, a 1-year-old would go in for five separate visits to get his or her routine 1-year vaccinations rather than get them all on the same day as is practice now.
The order instructs agencies to take actions to advance the White House’s recommendations.
The executive order’s effect on pediatricians’ offices may be limited, though. State health departments, not the federal government, dictate school vaccine mandates and vaccination schedules. States consider federal recommendations when updating their vaccine schedules, but are not required to follow the White House’s guidance.
For instance, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in January recommended reducing the number of vaccines recommended to all children to 11, down from 17 in 2024 — which the executive order also recommends. Trump, Kennedy and the MAHA movement have long argued that kids in the United States get more vaccines than children in other Western nations.
But more than two dozen states and the District of Columbia have rejected the new CDC vaccine recommendations, with most of those following guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics instead, according to health policy research organization KFF.
That prior attempt to overhaul the childhood vaccine schedule was also blocked in court.
The order also includes guidance that vaccination for measles, mumps and rubella be divided into three separate shots for each disease once such products are domestically available. The current MMR vaccine is only available as a combined shot.
The vaccines will still likely be covered by insurance and the CDC’s Vaccines for Children program, White House officials told reporters Monday evening, but that is dependent on forthcoming guidance from HHS.
And recommendations from HHS would likely include ways to ensure that parents don’t have to pay more for co-pays from multiple visits, officials said.
The move drew sharp criticism from Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, a gastroenterologist by training who has clashed with the administration on the issue of vaccines. He said Trump does not have the expertise to make these changes and said the policy change would “increase hesitancy and make children less safe.”
“Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy said on the social platform X.
Public health experts worry that splitting up childhood vaccinations across multiple visits will make it difficult for children to receive the dozens of vaccine doses recommended in their first 18 years. Pediatricians now typically administer multiple vaccines per visit.
“This executive order is part of a troubling pattern by the administration to attempt to unilaterally change vaccine guidance, particularly for children, rather than relying on the transparent, scientific review,” said Jan Carney, president of the American College of Physicians.
Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association, said the policy could exacerbate already growing childhood vaccination gaps and lead to increased pediatric deaths. He noted that measles cases are currently at a 35-year high in the United States and that the U.S. saw a record number of pediatric flu deaths during the 2024-25 respiratory virus season since they started being reported in 2004. Both diseases are vaccine-preventable.
“The executive order will cause more confusion for parents and healthcare providers, reduce vaccination rates and increase the spread of vaccine-preventable illnesses,” Wimmer said in a statement.
The move comes as the CDC gets a new director. Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the Senate just days before the announcement in a mostly party-line vote. She was not present at Monday’s Oval Office event.
