sources.news_title: Trump Executive Order Reshapes Childhood Vaccine Schedule
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday to reshape the nation’s childhood vaccine schedule after earlier changes attempted by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. were blocked in court.
The order calls for splitting up childhood vaccines into three categories, with different recommendations for who should get them, and directs federal agencies to implement the changes. It also proposed splitting up multiple vaccine doses, which are now used to limit the number of shots children must get, into separate shots.
“This updated recommendation finally aligns the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world,” Trump said during the signing. “More importantly, it aligns us with common sense and knowledge.”
Trump was joined at the signing by Kennedy, deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health.
Trending
Earlier this year, Kennedy bypassed a panel of vaccine advisers to pare the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, although courts have blocked that move thus far.
Kennedy pledged that the Department of Health and Human Services would deliver on the executive order within 90 days.
“We will keep working with urgency until American parents can have confidence that the medical advice that their government gives them is worthy of their trust,” Kennedy said.
The NIH has been overseeing a research initiative to seek possible causes of autism, which Trump and health officials announced last September. The effort — which includes 13 grants to outside researchers — won’t conclude for another two years, but Bhattacharya said over the weekend NIH will release some early results “in a couple weeks.”
“It’s not going to be a simple answer,” he said Sunday on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”
Trump, who harbors his own vaccine skepticism, has lately been pressuring Kennedy to move faster and more aggressively on enacting more changes to the childhood vaccine schedule and probing a repeatedly debunked link between vaccines and autism, according to news reports.
Yet White House officials have also sought to throttle Kennedy’s antivaccine proclivities. Both he and Bhattacharya have said in the past week that children should generally get vaccinated when questioned in television interviews about the worst measles outbreak in decades.
Bhattacharya said the order restores “autonomy of families and parents to make good decisions for their kids.”
In January, Kennedy appointed members to a federal autism advisory board who have been involved with antivaccine organizations or questioned the safety of the shots. The advisory board, created in 2000 to develop strategic plans for autism research and services, is scheduled to meet later this month.
“Nothing bad can happen from what we’re doing,” Trump said Monday. “Nothing bad can happen.”

sources.news_title: President Trump Signs Executive Order That Establishes “Gold Standard’ Childhood Vaccine Schedule * The Gateway Pundit * by Cristina Laila
sources.text:
President Trump on Monday signed an executive order establishing a new “gold standard” childhood vaccine schedule.
“Today, we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s Gold Standard Childhood Vaccination Recommendations and that has to do with many subjects but including autism in particular,” Trump said.
“Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today,” Trump said. “In those times, people were much healthier and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So, there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism. And we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was.”
“While we do not know exactly what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world,” Trump added.
“So we’re reducing them, we’re changing it to visits over the period of a year, a year and a half, so they get 20% of what they would have gotten in one big shot.”
“In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children,” President Trump said.
“Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases…” he said.
WATCH:
Read the executive order here:
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. Pursuant to the Presidential Memorandum of December 5, 2025 (Aligning United States Core Childhood Vaccine Recommendations with Best Practices from Peer, Developed Countries), the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) completed a scientific assessment, which identified a set of consensus vaccines that are consistently recommended in all peer countries and found that the United States currently recommends more childhood vaccines than any peer nation, including more than twice as many vaccine doses as some European nations (scientific assessment). The scientific assessment also found that, instead of implementing vaccination mandates, most peer nations maintain high childhood vaccination rates through public trust and education. In the United States, by contrast, individual States set mandatory vaccination requirements that children must meet to attend school.
Executive Order 14407 of May 29, 2026 (Realigning United States Core Childhood Vaccine Recommendations With Best Practices From Peer, Developed Countries), committed the Federal Government to ensuring that Americans are receiving the best scientifically supported medical advice in the world, as well as to protecting religious liberty and parental authority. However, implementation of my Administration’s prior directives regarding childhood vaccines has been delayed due to litigation over the composition of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and separate updates to the Federal vaccine schedule. Therefore, I am taking further action to reaffirm that it is the policy of the United States that the core childhood vaccine recommendations should be aligned with scientific evidence and best practices from peer, developed countries while preserving access to vaccines currently available to Americans. Further, it is the policy of my Administration that Federal programs and funding should support maximal parental choice over childhood vaccines, consistent with the Federal Government’s constitutional and statutory obligations and the fundamental principles of personal autonomy and informed consent.
Sec. 2. Recommendations for Childhood and Adolescent Vaccines. (a) Based on consultation with my advisors and review of available scientific evidence, it is hereby declared that the United States recognizes Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations informed by the three distinct categories of childhood immunization recommendations identified in the scientific assessment, as specified below:
(i) immunizations recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella;
(ii) immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations: respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue; and
(iii) immunizations based on shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza, and COVID-19.
(b) The Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations also recognize that the combined measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine should be administered in three separate single-disease shots once such products are domestically available and that, to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.
(c) Each executive department and agency shall review the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations and take any appropriate steps to advance them, to the fullest extent allowable by law.
(d) States and territories are advised to review the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations and consider updating relevant laws and regulations that define the scope of immunization requirements for contexts such as school enrollment and attendance based on the scientific assessment and best practices from peer, developed countries.
(e) The United States will routinely reassess the Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations according to the findings of the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines as specified in section 3 of this order.
Sec. 3. Improving Vaccine Research and Options for American Parents. The Secretary of HHS, through the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, shall, within 90 days of the date of this order, present plans to the President through the Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy to, to the extent appropriate and consistent with applicable law:
(a) offer options to administer core childhood vaccines, starting with MMR, as single vaccines rather than combination products/doses, including by working with the private sector and other countries as appropriate, while guaranteeing continued availability of combination vaccines and those vaccines recommended for shared clinical decision-making;
(b) assess the ideal timing and sequencing of all core childhood vaccines and adjust the Federal childhood and adolescent vaccine schedule as appropriate based on gold‑standard science;
(c) develop additional alternative adjuvants to aluminum and conduct comparative safety and efficacy studies;
(d) ensure continuous evaluation of the risk/benefit profiles of all childhood vaccines based on United States and international data; and
(e) improve vaccine safety monitoring, transparency, and research.
Sec. 4. Maximizing Parental Choice over Childhood Vaccines. (a) The Attorney General shall take appropriate measures to further meritorious legal actions challenging State laws that conflict with States’ constitutional and Federal statutory obligations related to parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations, and equal protection under the law, including, to the extent applicable under Federal law, States’ obligations to provide religious and medical exemptions from childhood and adolescent immunization requirements.
(b) The Departments of Justice, Education, and HHS shall take appropriate action to ensure that their contractors and grantees, including States and localities, are compliant with their constitutional and Federal statutory obligations related to parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations, and equal protection under the law, including, to the extent applicable under Federal law, their obligations to provide religious and medical exemptions from childhood and adolescent immunization requirements.
Sec. 5. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
(b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
(c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.
(d) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Department of Health and Human Services.

Trump signs order reducing recommended childhood vaccines
WASHINGTON >> President Donald Trump signed an executive order today calling for fewer childhood vaccinations by limiting the inoculation schedule to 11 immunizations.
The order also recommended splitting the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering the shots at separate medical visits.
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had in January cut the U.S. immunization schedule to remove shots against six out of 17 diseases, a move halted by a federal court ruling. The Trump order says that the federal government will now only support the remaining 11 shots.
The American Academy of Pediatrics and vaccine maker Merck criticized the order.
Public health experts say the immunization schedule was based on decades of evidence showing that the vaccines could protect against serious illness and death, and that the number of shots reflects the specific health needs of Americans. They say reducing the recommended vaccines will leave more children vulnerable to preventable diseases.
“Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases, along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up,” Trump said during a White House signing ceremony.

The U.S. ended in January its longstanding guidance that all children receive vaccines against flu and three other diseases, a sweeping change that advances one of Kennedy’s long-term goals.
Kennedy, a longtime vaccine critic, has previously led efforts to drop universal recommendations for hepatitis B shots for children and reduce the list of recommended vaccines, citing links to autism that scientists have repeatedly debunked.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday establishing a new federal childhood vaccination framework that separates vaccines into universal, high-risk and shared-decision categories while directing agencies to expand parental choice, review vaccine timing and pursue separate MMR shots.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday establishing what his administration calls the “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” restructuring federal guidance on childhood immunizations and directing agencies to reassess vaccine timing, combination products and parental choice.
WATCH:
“Today, we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s Gold Standard Childhood Vaccination Recommendations and that has to do with many subjects but including autism in particular,” Trump said.
The order builds on a December 2025 presidential memorandum and a May 29, 2026, executive order that called for aligning U.S. childhood vaccination recommendations with practices in other developed countries.
According to the new order, the Department of Health and Human Services completed a scientific assessment that found the United States recommends more childhood vaccines than any peer country, including more than twice as many doses as some European nations.
The administration also said the assessment found that many peer countries maintain high vaccination rates through public education and trust rather than mandates, while U.S. school vaccination requirements are generally established by individual states.
Trump said the administration intends to move toward fewer vaccines being given at the same time and more medical visits spread across a longer period.
“So we’re reducing them, we’re changing it to visits over the period of a year, a year and a half, so they get 20% of what they would have gotten in one big shot,” Trump said.
“In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children,” he added.
The executive order identifies 11 immunizations as the core vaccines recommended for all children: measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella.
“Effective immediately, my administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases…” Trump said.
A second category covers immunizations recommended for certain high-risk groups or populations, including respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY and dengue.
A third category places hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID-19 under shared clinical decision-making.
The order also states that the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should eventually be administered as three separate single-disease shots once such products are available domestically.
It further directs that, to the maximum extent feasible, childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits.
Federal departments and agencies are instructed to review the new recommendations and take lawful steps to advance them. States and territories are also encouraged to review their vaccine laws and consider updating immunization requirements governing school enrollment and attendance.
The administration said the recommendations will be reassessed regularly based on findings from the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines.
That task force has been given 90 days to present plans to the president through the assistant to the president for domestic policy.
Among its assignments is developing options for administering core childhood vaccines as separate products, beginning with MMR, while maintaining access to existing combination vaccines.
The task force must also assess the timing and sequencing of core childhood vaccines, determine whether the federal childhood and adolescent schedule should be adjusted, study alternatives to aluminum-based adjuvants and conduct comparative safety and efficacy research.
Additional directives call for continuous evaluation of childhood vaccine risk-benefit profiles using U.S. and international data and for improvements in vaccine safety monitoring, transparency and research.
Trump also connected the new policy to concerns about autism, although the order itself does not establish a causal relationship between vaccines and autism.
“Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today,” Trump said. “In those times, people were much healthier and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So, there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism. And we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was.”
Trump acknowledged that the cause of autism remains uncertain.
“While we do not know exactly what the cause is with respect to autism, it is essential to our research efforts that we have the very best vaccine recommendations in the entire world,” he said.
The executive order also directs the Justice Department to support what it describes as meritorious legal challenges to state laws that may conflict with constitutional or federal statutory protections involving parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations and equal protection.
The Justice, Education and Health and Human Services departments are similarly directed to ensure that contractors and grant recipients, including states and localities, comply with applicable federal obligations involving parental authority and exemptions from childhood and adolescent vaccination requirements.
The administration said the new policy is intended to preserve access to vaccines currently available in the United States while expanding parental choice and aligning federal recommendations with what it describes as scientific evidence and practices in peer developed countries.
The order also states that it must be implemented consistent with existing law and available appropriations and does not create a new legally enforceable right or benefit.

According to a report from the New York Post, President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order aimed at sharply limiting the number of recommended childhood vaccines while raising alarm over the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot.
Standing in the Oval Office alongside Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the president declared that the MMR vaccine can be “quite lethal” when administered as a single dose and called for the three components to be given separately at different times.
The order formalizes the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s January recommendation that reduced the childhood immunization schedule from 17 vaccines down to 11 core shots targeting the most serious diseases. Trump said the change takes effect immediately and that the administration is recognizing only those “gold standard” recommendations, “along with the MMR, which hopefully will be split up.”
“The MMR we wanted in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal, and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective,” Trump stated. “So the MMR we want to have separate visits, separate times.”
He described the volume of vaccine material given to young children as resembling “the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body,” claiming that “bad things happen in many too many cases.” The president insisted parents retain the right to choose additional vaccines if they wish, while pointing to certain groups that “have virtually no problem with autism” and are “not big into the world of vaccines.”
Kennedy, a longtime critic of vaccine safety, did not directly link shots to autism but highlighted a sharp rise in diagnoses among children born around 1989 or later. “We’re only noticing it in kids who were born around 1989 or after. The older generations are not seeing those increases,” he said. “So something happened in the mid 90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure. You need an environmental toxin.”

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order to space out childhood vaccines — What the new plan means
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump on Monday (August 10) signed an executive order seeking changes to federal childhood vaccine recommendations, including a push to separate some vaccines into different shots and medical visits.
The move reflects Trump's long-standing view that children should receive vaccines separately rather than getting multiple shots during the same visit.
However, public health experts have warned that delaying doses could leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases.
Here is what the executive order means and what could change.
The executive order, AP report cited The Daily Caller, directs the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to pursue revised childhood vaccine recommendations and expand vaccine research.
According to a White House fact sheet, the administration reportedly wants to promote separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three individual shots given at separate medical visits.
There is an important practical hurdle: separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not currently available for children in the US.
Trump also said at the Oval Office that one-year-old children should have their vaccinations spread across five separate visits. It was not immediately clear whether he meant all vaccines given at that age or only certain vaccinations.
Trump has repeatedly argued that children receive too many vaccines or too many shots at once.
The new order is part of a broader effort by the administration to revisit how vaccines are recommended, including the timing and combination of childhood immunisations.
The administration also wants HHS to improve research into vaccines and examine how other countries structure their vaccination recommendations.
However, childhood vaccine schedules are based on clinical studies that assess not only whether individual vaccines are safe, but also when they should be given and whether they can safely be administered together.
Public health experts have raised concerns that separating vaccines could create longer gaps in children's protection.
If a child receives one vaccine but has to return weeks or months later for another, there is a greater period during which the child could contract a disease that could otherwise have been prevented.
This is particularly significant for diseases such as measles, which is highly contagious.
Experts also note that requiring several additional medical appointments could make it harder for families to complete the recommended vaccination schedule.
No.
The federal government does not have the power to directly impose vaccination requirements for children attending schools.
Individual states determine school vaccination requirements, including which vaccines children must receive and what exemptions are available.
The White House fact sheet says the executive order will encourage states with school vaccine mandates to consider changing their laws to reflect the administration's revised recommendations.
Whether states actually change their requirements remains up to individual state governments.
The latest order follows another Trump directive issued in December 2025, when he instructed HHS to examine how other countries approach childhood vaccine recommendations and consider changes to US guidance.
HHS subsequently reduced the number of vaccines it recommended for every child.
That move, however, has since been blocked by a court.
Monday's executive order therefore represents another attempt by the administration to reshape federal vaccine policy.
The new vaccine policy is closely linked to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long questioned aspects of US vaccine policy.
Trump has also repeatedly pressed Kennedy to investigate the causes of autism.
At a Cabinet meeting last month, Trump publicly asked Kennedy:
“How are you doing on the autism research?”
Kennedy responded: “We will have an answer for you.”
On Monday, Kennedy again said he believes an unidentified environmental factor is responsible for the rise in autism diagnoses and said his department would release research findings when they are ready.
The scientific evidence is clear: decades of research have found no causal link between childhood vaccines and autism.
The MMR-autism claim gained prominence after a now-discredited study was published in the late 1990s. The study was subsequently withdrawn, and numerous large studies have failed to establish a link between vaccination and autism.
The current scientific consensus is that vaccines do not cause autism.
The executive order comes as children across the US return to school and amid a measles outbreak.
Health experts have warned that the outbreak could threaten the country's measles elimination status.
Measles is extremely contagious, and high vaccination coverage is considered essential for preventing sustained transmission.
That makes any changes to the timing or availability of childhood vaccines particularly consequential.
The executive order does not immediately replace the country's entire childhood vaccination schedule.
HHS will need to work through the process of developing or revising recommendations, while states will decide whether to change their own school vaccination requirements.
(With AP inputs)

sources.news_title: Trump signs executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots. Follow live updates. - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
President Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that certain shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order will recommend separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots administered in separate visits, and direct the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research.
See a recap.
Trump spokesperson suggests separating MMR vaccine could help instill trust in the vaccines — 8:26 p.m.
By the Associated Press
White House spokesperson Kush Desai said Monday that Trump’s call for the development of separate, single-disease measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for U.S. children will help generate trust in vaccine hesitant parents.
“President Trump is one of countless parents who have voiced questions and concerns about the combined MMR vaccine,” Desai told The Associated Press, saying the separate vaccines will “give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children, which ultimately will increase vaccination rates for all three diseases.”
The White House didn’t provide new scientific evidence supporting the move. Studies of babies and toddlers in the U.S. have shown that the use of combination shots increased the likelihood of completing all recommended vaccinations by the age of 2.
Pediatricians say executive order spreads confusion about vaccines, which are safe — 5:17 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Doctors from the American Academy of Pediatrics said the executive order spreads uncertainty and confusion.
Dr. Aaron Milstone, pediatric director of infection prevention at Johns Hopkins Health System, said doctors want to reassure parents there are “many, many, many years of scientific data highlighting the safety of vaccines in children.”The timing of vaccines has also been well-studied, he said.
“We give vaccines to children even when they’re young because we know that’s safe and because we know it’s the best time for their body to respond to that vaccine in a good way and to make their body stronger to fight off an infection if they’re exposed to that,” Milstone said.
The potential link between vaccines and autism has also also been studied exhaustively — in more than 40 well-designed studies in more than seven countries involving over five million children, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of American Academy of Pediatrics.
“I’m not sure that there is anything that has been as thoroughly looked at as this question about whether or not there is a link between autism and vaccines,” he said. “And the answer is unequivocally no.”
Republican senator blasts Trump executive order on vaccines — 5:11 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican, is strongly rebuking Trump’s executive order on vaccines.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” Cassidy said in a social media post on X. “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”
Cassidy chairs the Senate committee with oversight responsibilities for health care agencies. He went on to say that children will have to get more shots to get the same protection. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.
“Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy said.
Trump did not provide new evidence of a claimed link between vaccines and autism — 4:46 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The National Institutes of Health started funding research teams over a year ago charged with unearthing the cause autism, a portion of them assessing vaccines’ claimed role.
Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the head of the institute, spoke at Trump’s executive order signing and said that “science takes time” and “you don’t get answers immediately.”
Still, Bhattacharya was more tentative about claiming an evidence-based link between autism and vaccines, generally avoiding the suggestion altogether.
“What we’ve done in this administration,” he said, “is we’ve given permission to scientists to honestly answer this question, to find the link for the first time.”
Todd Blanche is sworn in as attorney general after bruising confirmation fight — 4:24 p.m.
By the Associated Press
President Trump’s former personal lawyer, Todd Blanche, was sworn in Monday as attorney general after a bruising confirmation fight that exposed bipartisan concerns about the Justice Department’s direction under the Republican president.
Another former Trump attorney — Emil Bove, now a federal appeals court judge — administered the oath of office to Blanche at the White House following early Saturday’s Senate confirmation vote by the narrowest of margins. Shortly after, the newly sworn-in attorney general arrived at Justice Department headquarters to cheers from employees lined up along the entrance.
Blanche, a former federal prosecutor in New York, is officially taking command of a Justice Department he has been leading in an acting capacity since Pam Bondi’s firing in April.
12 medical groups previously endorsed the childhood influenza vaccine. Trump’s executive order did not — 4:19 p.m.
By the Associated Press
In January, the American Academy of Pediatrics put out their 2026 childhood vaccine guidance, which included a jab for influenza, that got the green light from groups including the National Medical Association and Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society.
The AAP said in a press release at the time that over 80% of childhood deaths related to influenza were with unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated patients, adding that children under 5 years old are particularly vulnerable.
Trump said the vaccine is “no longer recommended for all children.”
Trump says Iran can still cause trouble but argues that it’s feeling financial squeeze — 4:07 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president was dismissive of Iranian officials’ demands after Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei stressed that Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the U.S. meets its conditions, including paying reparations for the five-month-old war.
Trump during an Oval Office exchange with reporters claimed that the U.S. has “100% control” of the strait, but that the situation remains complex. He made the case that the U.S. Navy’s blockade of the strait is preventing Iran from selling its oil on the international market, a move that is effectively choking the Iranian economy.
“Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble, but they’re broke,” Trump said. “They have no money. You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And they’re not paying their soldiers.”
With measles raging, vaccine proponent said it’s no time for an ‘anti-vaccine agenda’ — 3:59 p.m.
By the Associated Press
At a time when the U.S. is facing its worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years, “we should be making it easier to protect children from preventable disease, not harder,” said Northe Saunders, president of American Families for Vaccines.
He said “RFK’s anti-vaccine agenda” shouldn’t pressure state leaders to abandon protections that work for their communities.
“States have long played a central role in setting school immunization requirements,” he said. “and parents, educators, healthcare professionals, and state leaders should be able to make decisions about protecting children without political interference from the federal government.”
In late July, the number of measles cases in the U.S. has surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has logged more than 2,318 cases of measles this year.
Trump’s childhood vaccine recommendations contradict medical establishment — 3:58 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president, at an executive order signing on new childhood vaccine recommendations, said that, “very importantly,” jabs for hepatitis B, COVID-19 and influenza “are no longer recommended for all children.”
Those vaccinations, however, are still recommended by the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics, among other medical groups.
While the latter organization recommends childhood vaccines for 18 diseases, Trump’s executive order limits that to prioritizing just 11.
Public health officials have raised concerns over some of Trump’s recommendations — 3:46 p.m.
By the Associated Press
That includes the presidents recommendation announced Monday to space out childhood vaccine shots instead of getting all of them on the same visit.
Public health officials say that could lead to children becoming infected with a vaccine-preventable disease in the periods between jabs.
Doctor urges parents to listen to medical experts about shots — 3:45 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Michael Osterholm, executive director of the Vaccine Integrity Project, said parents should continue to rely on vaccine recommendations developed by trusted medical and public health experts, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, when making decisions on shots for their kids.
“Today’s Executive Order does not change the underlying scientific evidence supporting childhood immunization. That data has been built over decades — through large clinical trials, real-world effectiveness studies and continuous safety monitoring involving millions of children,” he said in a statement.
“Parents deserve clear, evidence-based guidance about how to protect their children, not competing recommendations issued through political processes. When families receive conflicting messages, confidence in vaccination suffers, and children ultimately bear the consequences.”
Trump overstates dangers of vaccines — 3:33 p.m.
By the Associated Press
In announcing his executive order on vaccines, President Trump said “bad things happen” when children get the combined MMR vaccine.
“I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination that looks like the size of a bottle of soda poured into a little child’s body, and bad things happen in, many cases-in too many cases,” he said.
But experts say the risk of serious side effects is extremely low and years of real-world data proves the vaccine is safe and effective. Common side effects include soreness and a mild rash or redness at the injection site, a fever, and temporary pain or stiffness in the joints.
Decades of studies have concluded there’s no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
Decades of autism research have found no single cause — 3:24 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Besides genetics, scientists have identified various possible factors, including the age of a child’s father, the mother’s weight, and whether she had diabetes or was exposed to certain chemicals.
Any concern that vaccines could be linked to autism has been long debunked, according to scientists and leading advocacy groups for people with autism.
Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Trump proposes new childhood vaccine recommendations, though power in schools rests with states — 3:23 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump, who suggested connections between autism and vaccines despite a scientific consensus that their isn’t a link, issued new guidance for childhood vaccines that space out shots and limit the number of recommended routine jabs.
Still, the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren rests with state governments.
Trump to sign executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots — 3:00 p.m.
By the Associated Press
President Trump on Monday will sign an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits, according to a White House fact sheet.
The order will recommend administering each vaccine in its own visit and separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots and direct the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research, says the fact sheet, first reported by The Daily Caller. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for children are not available in the US.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit.
CBO says this year’s deficit will be larger than previously predicted, mostly because of smaller-than-expected tariff revenue — 2:39 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The Congressional Budget Office is projecting that this fiscal year’s deficit will be $2.1 trillion, about $200 billion more than what it predicted in early February.
The major reason for the change has to do with less revenue coming into the Treasury than projected as a result of the Supreme Court finding that the tariffs President Donald Trump imposed under an emergency powers law were unconstitutional.
The fiscal year runs through September 30.
Revenue totaled $4.5 trillion through the first 10 months of the fiscal year. That’s about 3 percent more than during the same period a year ago.
Meanwhile, spending increased about 5 percent from last year, rising to $6.3 trillion. Spending in the federal government’s major health care programs, Medicare and Medicaid, each increased by about 8 percent.
Trump signs waiver letting foreign trips carry oil and other goods among US ports for 90 days — 2:07 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump on Monday extended a waiver for 90 days for foreign ships to transport goods, including oil, fertilizers and other fossil fuel products, among US ports.
The president first waived the Jones Act on March 17 so that it would be easier to transport oil and refined fuels among ports, reducing price pressures after the start of the war with Iran.
The extension will take effect on August 17.
Unlike previous extensions, the Pentagon will consult with the Maritime Administration to decide which voyages are exempt from the 1920 law containing the Jones Act. The waiver will only apply to cargo are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture and food, such as soybean oil.
Trump concedes there was ‘some contractor error’ at Reflecting Pool — 2:06 p.m.
By the New York Times
President Trump on Sunday said on social media that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s problems were caused in part by “some contractor error done by rushing the job for a July 4th opening.”
It was a change in rhetoric for the president, who had spent weeks falsely blaming the pool’s problems on vandals.
In his social media post, Trump also conceded that there was “no video or proof” to back up the assertions that vandalism damaged the pool. Still, he continued to blame one of the people who had been charged with vandalism, David Hearn, a former U.S. Olympian. Hearn had been charged with a felony by U.S. attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office before his case was dropped.
Ex Air Force secretary talking to lawyers after Trump admin revokes security clearance — 1:47 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall said Monday that he’s talking to lawyers after the Trump administration revoked his security clearance last week.
Kendall, who has been critical of the administration, said in a post on LinkedIn that he’s “talking to lawyers and will have more soon.” He said he’s had his clearance for 60 years and was careful to say nothing classified.
The Pentagon revoked Kendall’s “eligibility” to access classified information and barred him from holding “any sensitive position,” alleging Friday that he disclosed sensitive information about Air Force One’s capabilities to the media.
It follows reporting last month, including from The New York Times, on security concerns over the new, Qatari-gifted Air Force One, including that it lacked the advanced antimissile capabilities of its predecessor.
US military base in South Carolina renamed after late Senator Lindsey Graham — 1:33 p.m.
By the Associated Press
A U.S. military base in South Carolina was renamed after the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham Monday, with Defense Department Sec. Pete Hegseth praising Graham’s dedication to the military and for “taking on a radical leftist ideology” in the armed forces.
Joint Base Charleston is now Joint Base Lindsey Graham, which includes an Air Force base and a Naval Weapons Station. Graham, who died last month, served in the Air Force, Air National Guard and reserves.
Hegseth praised Graham’s support of President Trump’s historic $1.5 billion defense budget proposal. In praising Graham, Hegseth also employed the Trump administration’s strategy of linking Democrats to communism.
“The hard left declared war on our own military,” Hegseth said, adding that “it seems that many people have forgotten the reality of what communism looks like.”
Trump dismisses Iran’s call for war reparations — 1:29 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump is scoffing at the Iran’s call for reparations for devastation caused to the country by the U.S. and Israeli bombardment over the last five months, a demand he said hadn’t been raised by Tehran’s negotiators until now.
The Republican president, in a social media post, added that in response to the Iranian demand he’s directing negotiators to include “compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts.”
The U.S. government says Iran-backed militants have been responsible for the deaths and injuries of hundreds of Americans over the last several decades, including the 1983 bombing on Marine compound in Beirut that killed 241 U.S. military personnel, the 1996 truck bombing a U.S. Air Force housing complex in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. troops and wounded hundreds more, and the deaths of at least 603 U.S. troops in Iraq between 2003 and 2011.
Trump announces staff secretary Will Scharf will be his new White House counsel — 12:15 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump announced Sunday that his new White House counsel will be Will Scharf, the staff secretary who as the Trump-appointed head of the National Capital Planning Commission helped secure approval for the $400 million ballroom project.
Trump said that, beginning Sept. 1, Scharf will be replacing David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the Supreme Court.
“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”
The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture — just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican Party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress. Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.
Trump officials propose new scrutiny of food additives and ingredients — 12:07 p.m.
By the Associated Press
U.S. health officials on Monday proposed a rule change that would require food manufacturers to notify regulators before introducing new ingredients or additives into processed or packaged foods.
The proposal would change a decades-old policy that advocates have called a regulatory loophole, blaming it for allowing thousands of unvetted ingredients into the U.S. food supply.
Under the proposed rule from the Food and Drug Administration, companies would have to document and submit their safety findings for new ingredients, giving regulators the opportunity to investigate if they see a potential safety risk. Currently companies can decide for themselves if an ingredient or additive is “generally recognized as safe” and there is no requirement for companies to notify or submit evidence to the FDA, although some do.
State Department says it has revoked more 175,000 visas since Trump took office — 11:52 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The revoked visas had been granted to more than 175,000 foreigners who have endangered American citizens, broken laws or threatened U.S. national security, according to a statement issued Monday by the State Department.
The statement says most were revoked “due to law enforcement encounters for a range of criminal activity,” including assault, child abuse, drunken driving, drug violations, and embezzlement. It doesn’t say how many of those visa holders had been convicted of such crimes.
Some of the revocations involved “foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk, including one who stated ‘when fascists die, democrats don’t complain’ and another who said he ‘died too late’, the statement said.
Veteran Democrats face strong challenges in Connecticut’s primary — 11:41 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Democratic Gov. Ned Lamont’s try for a third term must first clear a challenge by state Rep. Josh Elliott. And U.S. Rep. John Larson faces his first primary challenge in nearly 30 years, from former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune and state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest.
Both contests could help redefine the Democratic brand by replacing old guard figures with younger alternatives. Tuesday’s primaries also could extend a progressive winning streak in New York City, Colorado and the Michigan U.S. Senate primary.
Larson turned 78 in July. Concerns over his health and age arose last year after he suffered a seizure while delivering a speech on the House floor.
What to expect in Vermont’s state primary — 11:25 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Vermont Democrats will try on Tuesday to do something they’ve been unable to do in five previous attempts: nominate a gubernatorial candidate who can beat Republican Gov. Phil Scott.
Voters will also decide contested Democratic primaries for lieutenant governor and state auditor and choose a Republican nominee to challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Becca Balint in November.
Scott is one of only two Republican governors to serve a state Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election. But he’s been a rare Republican critic of Trump, and he received 73% of the vote for his 2024 reelection.
Two Democrats are running to challenge Scott: economist Amanda Janoo and former child advocacy organization CEO Aly Richards, who boasts endorsements from former Democratic Govs. Howard Dean and Madeleine Kunin.
Iranian leadership makes display of unity against US — 11:23 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Iran’s president says the country’s supreme leader is calling for “unity and cohesion” as its war with the United Statesbrings more economic hardships to the Islamic Republic.
President Masoud Pezeshkian described a nearly seven-hour meeting with Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in an interview Monday with Iranian state television that aired amid apparent tensions among the Islamic Republic’s leaders.
He told IRIB they discussed people’s livelihoods, the state of the market, employment, people’s housing and problems resulting from U.S. sanctions. Most important, he said, was Khamenei’s emphasis on unity.
“All of the enemy’s plans are aimed at creating division,” Pezeshkian said. “What we have to do is prevent divisions from emerging.”
He didn’t say when or where they met. Khamenei is believed to have been wounded in the U.S.-Israeli strike that killed his father and has not appeared in public since he was appointed in March.
Judge cancels release hearing for 1st person ever charged in 30-year-old Alien Terrorist Removal Court — 11:12 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A federal judge has canceled a release hearing this week for Afghan woman who is the first person ever charged in a 30-year-old deportation court that was recently activated by the Trump administration.
A Tuesday hearing had been set in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court’s inaugural case against Nazira Haji Zada, who is accused of supporting the Islamic State group. But the court’s chief judge agreed Monday to give her lawyers more time to prepare and gather information. A new hearing date wasn’t immediately set.
The court received its first-ever petition when the Justice Department filed an application seeking Haji Zada’s removal, opening an untested new front in Trump’s deportation campaign. Haji Zada, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, wants to be released from custody while the court case is pending.
Democrats face tougher reelection fights in redrawn districts — 10:40 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The court-inspired actions in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee, as well as earlier legislative actions in other states to redraw boundaries through unusual mid-decade redistricting, were part of a nationwide Republican effort championed by Trump to maximize the party’s chances of holding its slim U.S. House majority this year.
Candidates in Tuesday’s special primaries in Alabama are running under the new Republican-backed boundaries, which go into effect in January 2027. Both Democratic representatives are unopposed in their party primaries, but facing tougher odds in November.
Rep. Shomari Figures, for example, was elected in a district where Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris beat Trump 53% to 46%. In his newly drawn district, Trump would have beaten Harris 57% to 42%.
What to expect in primaries for Alabama’s redistricted congressional seats — 10:30 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Voters in four of Alabama’s seven congressional districts select U.S. House nominees in special primaries Tuesday under a new map that eliminates one of the state’s two majority-Black districts currently represented by Democrats.
Republican Gov. Kay Ivey had postponed contests for the 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts following a U.S. Supreme Court decision that prompted a handful of Republican-controlled Southern states to throw out their congressional maps.
What to expect as South Carolina voters choose Sen. Lindsey Graham’s successor— 10:00 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Ten Republicans are competing in Tuesday’s special primary election, including two congressmen, a former governor and Graham’s sister, now a U.S. senator appointed to serve out the final months of his current term.
Lindsey Graham’s unexpected death, a month after winning the June 9 Republican primary for the seat he first won a quarter-century ago, created this vacancy for the GOP’s nominee on the November ballot for another six-year term.
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham has Trump’s endorsement. Her opponents include Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman, former Gov. Mark Sanford and business owner Mark Lynch, who ran against Lindsey Graham in the June 9 primary.
If no candidate receives a majority, the top two vote-getters advance to a special primary runoff on Aug. 25. The winner will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician.
Washington grapples with a National Guard deployment extended until 2029 — 9:50 a.m.
By the Associated Press
It’s been 12 months since Trump announced a crime emergency in Washington, pledging to make the city “safe and beautiful” and deploying the National Guard.
But a mission that seemed temporary has been extended through January 2029. Residents and a new cadre of local officials consider it an unacceptable federal attempt to restrict the heavily Democratic city’s autonomy. A year in, they still question the necessity of troops on the streets of the nation’s capital.
“Here we are in the capital of the free world, and our president is treating it like a police state,” said Scott Michelman, legal director of the ACLU of the District of Columbia.
The continued deployment will be a major test for the politicians taking office after this year’s elections — residents will want them to use their limited powers to push back on Republican encroachment into the city’s affairs.
White House mum on Israel’s rejection of Trump’s Gaza deal — 8:55 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The White House has not commented on the Israeli Prime Minister’s dismissal of Trump’s deal for Gaza. Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel’s military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting that “Israel rejects the 15-point document” but is still discussing plans for Gaza with Washington. Trump had said Israeli forces would withdraw as the Hamas militant group’s disarmament is completed. Israeli forces control over half the Palestinian enclave of about 2 million people that’s been largely destroyed.
“We remain committed to the road map,” said a member of the Hamas political bureau, Bassem Naim, adding that the group expects mediators and the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu — who also faces domestic tensions as he struggles to hold onto power ahead of the next elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
Ocasio-Cortez says she’s freezing her eggs as she decides her next political moves — 8:50 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The 36-year-old Democratic New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez explained her decision in an ABC “This Week” interview on Sunday and said she has not ruled out running for president or for the U.S. Senate seat held by the Democrats’ floor leader, Chuck Schumer.
Ocasio-Cortez says in her social media posts that she’s taking a political risk in sharing such a personal decision about her potential plans to have children. The congresswoman says she wants to feel more control over her life and normalize conversations about what women face in their professional and personal lives.
Iran presses demands on US as shipping standoff grinds on — 8:15 a.m.
By the Associated Press
An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets its conditions.
“It is up to the U.S. side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions,” Esmail Baghaei said Monday, noting the American blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran wants the U.S. to lift its blockade on the Strait, pay compensation for months of war damage, lift economic sanctions and release Iran’s frozen assets. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a waterway that normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world’s traded oil supplies — has become the war’s most lasting consequence. The impasse has kept energy prices as a major focus of U.S. politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Iran is holding separate talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including potentially a temporary shipping corridor. But it has said any actual reopening is contingent on talks with the U.S.
Trump’s immigration crackdown looms over Minnesota’s bruising Senate primary — 7:55 a.m.
By the Associated Press
In the streets surrounding a drab federal office complex next to the Minneapolis airport, the beleaguered resistance to President Trump found its footing.
As U.S. immigration agents staged at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building for a monthslong deportation campaign, protesters with whistles and cellphone cameras assembled to oppose them. Two were shot and killed in the city’s streets before Trump pulled back under pressure.
Months later, those confrontations remain the backdrop to Minnesota’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, which features establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Trump signs executive order calling for spacing out childhood shots
Published 2:45 pm Monday, August 10, 2026
President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order calling for revamped childhood vaccine recommendations that promote his long-held belief that childhood shots should be spaced out into separate medical visits.
The order recommends separating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three different shots administered in separate visits, and directs the nation’s health department to improve vaccine research, says a White House fact sheet, first reported by The Daily Caller. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines for children are not currently available in the United States.
Speaking about the order at the Oval Office on Monday, Trump also said that one-year-olds should have their shots separated out into five separate visits, though it wasn’t clear whether he was talking about all the vaccines they receive or specific ones.
Public health experts have raised concerns that spacing out shots as Trump suggests can lead to an increased risk that children become infected with a vaccine-preventable disease before returning for another visit. Childhood vaccines — and how and when to give them in combination — go through rigorous studies, and safety tracking continues for years as the shots are used.
Even as the order calls for revised vaccine recommendations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren. The order will advise states with school vaccine mandates to consider updating their laws to reflect the administration’s recommendations, the fact sheet said.
Last December, Trump ordered HHS to review how peer nations approach vaccine recommendations and consider revising U.S. guidance accordingly. The department responded by cutting the number of vaccines it recommends for every child, a move that has since been blocked in court.
In the months leading up to Monday’s announcement, Trump’s administration had largely pivoted away from talking about vaccine policy in favor of less polarizing topics like healthy eating and efforts to lower drug prices ahead of November’s elections. Polls show most Americans still support school vaccine requirements, though Republicans are less likely than Democrats to see them as important.
Still, Trump has been fixated on connecting autism to vaccines. He has recently ramped up pressure on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to identify the cause of autism, something Kennedy had pledged to do with new research unveiled last year. Trump publicly prodded the health secretary for an update on autism research in a Cabinet meeting last month.
“How are you doing on the autism research?” Trump asked.
“We will have an answer for you,” Kennedy said.
Scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between childhood vaccines and autism. On Monday, Kennedy repeated his assertion that he believes an unknown environmental factor is to blame for rising autism diagnoses and said that his department will deliver research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
Monday’s order comes as school years are starting around the country and the nation contends with a measles outbreak that experts say could result in the U.S. losing its measles elimination status.

sources.news_title: Trump returns to controversial vaccine policy with order questioning childhood schedule
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration, which in recent months had avoided public discussions of vaccine policy because of concern around the political repercussions, is changing course.
Speaking from the Oval Office, President Trump on Monday unveiled a new executive order as he and his top health officials presented a new, skeptical government approach to vaccines, making extraordinary claims without evidence to support the remade federal agenda.
“That’s a big one in my book,” Trump said after signing the order.
The executive order lists vaccines to be recommended for all children, those at high risk of infection, or just in consultation with a clinician — a stark change from the usually public, scientist-led process of determining the federal government’s approach to immunization issues. The new “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations” were instead made in consultation with the president’s advisers and relied on comparing the U.S. system to those in other countries. (The White House did not answer questions about why that approach was taken and who advised the president on the order.)
The order recommends all children get 11 vaccines instead of the 18 previously recommended by the federal government — and would spread out the doses over a longer time, the president said. The administration did not provide immunological evidence for the changed schedule.
The order was a response to a court stalling previous changes to vaccine policy, Heidi Overton, a health policy adviser at the White House, said.
After the order was signed, a White House official told reporters on a call that the new policy complies with previous court orders and would prevail in future challenges because the president has the right to make recommendations of “what he understands the best view of the science and the gold standard for vaccination to be.”
The order also calls for the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps, and rubella, to be broken up into three vaccines. That wouldn’t be possible, experts say, without years of work and investment to make a change not supported by evidence.
Still, the president said without evidence that the vaccine could be “quite lethal” in its combined form, despite the shot being repeatedly proven safe through large-scale studies. Later, Trump backtracked, saying there isn’t evidence that the shot is lethal but adding that he had heard the claim from others.
Overton later clarified that the administration recommends the shot for all children.
Asked why the president recommended splitting up the MMR vaccine, one White House official pointed to a review from two Kennedy-chosen advisers — but the review recommends the shot and doesn’t discuss splitting it into separate vaccines.
Though Trump said he does not know the cause of rising autism rates, he and other officials connected the vaccine order to their efforts to understand and stop the growth of the disorder.
Trump said parents could still get their children vaccines if they wish and that insurance would continue covering the shots.
A host of health experts — and at least one Republican lawmaker — decried the new order, saying it lacks evidence supporting the changes.
“This executive order is wrong,” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who leads the Senate’s health panel, said in a social media post. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes.”
Cassidy previously said he had levers to hold the administration to account after voting to confirm two new health officials.
The president directed the federal health department’s Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to issue a report on evidence on the assertions made by the president in the order, such as splitting up the MMR vaccine, as well as on how to implement the White House directive.
Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the agency had already launched “unprecedented” research efforts in vaccines.
The order may not necessarily translate into real changes in vaccination practices — at least not at the national level. Hospitals and doctors have chosen to ignore previous vaccine recommendations from the Trump administration, arguing federal officials aren’t offering evidence to back up policy overhauls.
It’s the latest in a series of actions from the administration returning to highlighting concerns — even those at odds with established medical guidance — with current vaccination practices.
Earlier this month, Kennedy lashed out during an interview on CNN over vaccine and public health policies. Days before the appearance, the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was pushing for more actions on vaccines. In May, the president signed an executive order pressing federal health agencies to continue changing the nation’s framework.
The Trump administration was previously skittish about publicly touting its changes to vaccine policy. A Trump pollster presented evidence that “vaccine skepticism is bad politics,” and the administration focused on health care affordability over the sweeping changes it was overseeing across federal shot regulations. At the time, one White House official said the administration was “done” with its work on vaccines.
Now, officials say, that’s changing.
Asked if there’s been a shift, Calley Means, a senior adviser at HHS, said in a text message: “Gloves are off.”
The shift, if effective in changing vaccinations across the country, could have profound effects on the health of Americans, especially children. The administration has considered far-reaching policies that could upend the vaccine market — though the most extreme ideas have yet to make it into federal policy.
Kennedy has for years been critical of vaccinations, sharing debunked theories about the shots and warning parents to keep their kids vaccine-free. Trump himself also has a history of expressing doubts about vaccine safety. (Scientists and doctors have repeatedly used large bodies of evidence to show the safety and effectiveness of the shots when approving them.)
Kennedy led the Make America Healthy Again movement that was made up in part by other vaccine skeptics — many of whom were concerned by the administration sidestepping the issue publicly. The shift may be seen as a win for MAHA leaders who have worked to build support in the administration to not shy away from the issue. Trump thanked “MAHA moms” in particular when introducing the order on Monday.
The shift also presents a potential challenge for the incoming CDC director, Erica Schwartz.
Schwartz, during her Senate confirmation hearing just last month, assured lawmakers she would “follow the science” — but didn’t directly answer questions about whether she would stand up to administration leaders if necessary.
This story has been updated with additional information on the White House’s plans.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) said breaking up the MMR vaccine would mean children getting more shots for the same protection.
“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” wrote Cassidy, who lost his reelection bid after Trump backed his primary challenger. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism.”

sources.news_title: Trump Preparing Order To Reshape Childhood Vaccine Guidance - American Liberty News
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is preparing another major intervention in U.S. vaccine policy, with the White House drafting an executive order expected to address childhood vaccination recommendations, autism research and parents’ role in deciding which vaccines their children receive.
The order remains under development and could change before Trump signs it, according to reports from The Washington Post and Bloomberg.
Bloomberg reported that the president wants to break up the combined measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine into three separate shots. The proposed order could also include additional changes implemented through executive action.
The effort would mark the latest attempt by Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to reshape federal vaccine policy after the administration already moved to dramatically narrow the number of vaccines routinely recommended for American children.
It also comes amid continued scrutiny of Trump and Kennedy’s statements about a possible connection between vaccines and autism, a link that has not been established by extensive scientific research.
New order could target childhood vaccine schedule
The precise language of the forthcoming order has not been publicly released.
People familiar with its development told The Washington Post that discussions have focused on the childhood immunization schedule, federal autism research, and expanding parental choice over vaccinations.
The White House has not publicly confirmed the final provisions.
Spokesman Kush Desai told the Post that the administration remains committed to using what it calls “gold standard science” to develop the country’s childhood vaccination policies.
The potential order would follow months of direct presidential involvement in an area of public health policy traditionally handled primarily through federal health agencies and outside medical experts.
A Congressional Research Service report published in June found no previous instance in which a president had directly ordered a review of or changes to the childhood immunization schedule.
Trump already ordered major vaccine overhaul
The latest proposal would not be Trump’s first effort to remake the childhood schedule.
In December 2025, Trump directed HHS and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to compare U.S. childhood vaccination practices with those of other developed countries and make changes if officials concluded those countries followed better practices.
Federal health officials subsequently unveiled a revised schedule in January that reduced the number of vaccines universally recommended for children from 17 to 11.
Under that approach, vaccines against measles, mumps, rubella, polio, pertussis, tetanus, diphtheria, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, HPV and chickenpox remained universally recommended.
The administration moved hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, meningococcal disease, RSV and rotavirus vaccines out of the universal category, instead placing them under recommendations for certain risk groups or shared decision-making between families and healthcare providers.
The administration said the changes brought American recommendations closer to those of peer countries while preserving access to vaccines for families that wanted them.
Major medical organizations strongly opposed the overhaul. The American Academy of Pediatrics said it would continue publishing its own recommendations, including some routine vaccinations removed from the federal universal schedule.
Federal judge blocked earlier changes
The administration’s vaccine overhaul soon encountered a significant legal obstacle.
U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked implementation of the revised childhood schedule in March as part of litigation challenging Kennedy’s changes to federal vaccine policy.
The ruling effectively restored the previous schedule while the case proceeded.
The federal government appealed the decision on April 29.
Trump responded in May with Executive Order 14407, which declared that U.S. childhood vaccine recommendations should be aligned with scientific evidence and practices in other developed countries while preserving Americans’ access to currently available vaccines.
The order instructed the CDC and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices to review the administration’s earlier assessment alongside current clinical data and take legally permissible steps toward updating the schedule.
The new order now being drafted could push the administration’s campaign further.
Autism expected to play prominent role
The most politically and scientifically contentious portion of the emerging initiative involves autism.
Trump has repeatedly questioned whether childhood vaccinations could contribute to autism and has pressed Kennedy for answers about what causes the developmental condition.
During a recent Cabinet meeting, Trump publicly asked Kennedy about his department’s autism research.
“We will have an answer for you,” Kennedy responded, according to reporting on the exchange.
The administration’s continuing interest comes despite extensive research finding no causal relationship between vaccines and autism.
The original controversy was fueled in part by a 1998 paper suggesting a connection between the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and autism. The paper was subsequently retracted, and its conclusions have not been supported by larger studies.
One of the most extensive studies, involving more than 650,000 children in Denmark, found no increased autism risk associated with the MMR vaccine.
Kennedy has long questioned the scientific consensus surrounding vaccine safety and autism, although his public emphasis has shifted during his tenure at HHS.
The forthcoming order reportedly calls for additional federal attention to autism research rather than declaring that vaccines cause autism.
Trump taking unusual role in vaccine policy
The administration’s approach represents a significant change not only in which vaccines Washington recommends but in how those recommendations are developed.
Before 2026, the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices traditionally played the leading role in developing the annual childhood schedule alongside federal health officials and outside medical organizations.
The January overhaul was instead developed by federal officials without the usual ACIP process, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Kennedy had previously removed all sitting members of ACIP and appointed a new group.
The combination of those personnel changes, Trump’s executive orders and the administration’s direct involvement in childhood vaccine recommendations has produced an increasingly fragmented system in which federal guidance and recommendations from major medical organizations may differ.
Final order has not been released
The most important details of Trump’s latest move remain unresolved.
The White House has not released a draft, and an executive order being prepared internally can be revised substantially or abandoned before the president signs it.
That means reports that Trump is preparing another vaccine order are independently corroborated, but claims about exactly which vaccines would be affected — or precisely what new recommendations the administration will impose — remain premature.
What is clear is that Trump is preparing to return to an issue his administration has already transformed.
After narrowing federal childhood vaccine recommendations, reorganizing the government’s vaccine advisory structure and battling medical groups in federal court, the White House is now considering another presidential order that could further reshape how Washington approaches childhood vaccination and autism research.
This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.
