Trump Order Seeks Vaccine Schedule Overhaul
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday urging states to reconsider school vaccine mandates and pushing to split the combined measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) shot into three separate injections.
Trump’s order functions as a non-binding advisory rather than a direct mandate because states have the direct authority to set school immunisation requirements.
The directive also instructs the Department of Health and Human Services to form a task force with the private sector to develop single-dose alternatives while maintaining access to combined vaccines.
Medical experts, public health officials, and politicians swiftly condemned the order as scientifically baseless and dangerous.
New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin criticised the policy for relying on politics and conspiracy theories, emphasising that cities and states set their own requirements.
Senator Bill Cassidy also denounced the move, warning that the president lacks the medical expertise to alter vaccine policy and that splitting shots will only increase vaccine hesitancy, putting children at risk.
The administration’s push aligns with the long-held agenda of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who continues to promote the disproven link between immunisations and autism.
Public health organisations, including the American Academy of Paediatrics, reaffirmed that decades of clinical data prove the combined MMR shot is safe, effective, and crucial for providing rapid immunity.
The executive order comes as a federal court continues to block previous administration attempts to overhaul vaccine policies and as the nation faces its worst measles outbreak in 35 years.

sources.news_title: American Academy of Paediatrics Blasts Donald Trump’s Children Vaccine Directive, Calls New Order ‘Disheartening And Dangerous’
Trump Vaccine Plan Recognizes Just 11 Diseases
sources.text:
The Trump vaccine plan now recognizes routine childhood immunization against just 11 diseases for all children, marking a major change in how the federal government categorizes vaccines that families have encountered for years. Trump vaccine to the White House executive order, those 11 are measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus and varicella.
Video
That does not mean children will receive only 11 shots, and it does not mean the previous federal schedule contained 72 separate vaccines. The number 72 came directly from Trump while promoting the change Monday. According to CBS News, Trump said, “In many cases, we were requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children.” The figure refers to his characterization of the number of doses children could receive under previous recommendations, not 72 different vaccine products.
Under the Trump vaccine plan, several immunizations that are not included in the 11 disease universal category remain part of federal guidance but are placed into different groups. The White House order places hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal vaccines, dengue protection and RSV monoclonal antibodies in a category for certain higher risk populations. Hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and COVID 19 are also listed under shared clinical decision making.
The framework builds on a federal shift that started earlier this year. According to the CDC, officials announced in January that the routine category would cover 11 diseases after HHS reviewed childhood vaccine schedules in 20 other developed nations. The agency said the United States previously recommended protection against 18 diseases and more total childhood doses than some of the countries reviewed.
Trump is now using an executive order to push that approach further. The Trump vaccine plan tells federal departments and agencies to review the new recommendations and take appropriate steps to advance them where permitted by law. The order also advises states and territories to consider whether their own vaccination rules, including requirements connected to school attendance, should be updated. States still maintain authority over their school immunization policies.
Another major change involves how vaccines could be administered. The order says the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should eventually be offered as three separate single disease shots once those products become available domestically. It also calls for childhood immunizations to be administered during separate medical visits whenever feasible. According to CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder, that MMR option currently does not exist in the United States. Merck stopped making the standalone measles, mumps and rubella vaccines in 2009,” Gounder said. “There’s no licensed version in this country. No company has said it’s building one, and the order only takes effect once those products exist.”
The Trump vaccine plan also orders HHS to examine the timing and sequencing of childhood vaccines and present plans within 90 days. According to the executive order, the HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines must also consider alternatives to aluminum adjuvants, continue evaluating vaccine safety and effectiveness data and strengthen vaccine safety monitoring and research.
Trump repeatedly brought autism into his remarks even though autism does not appear as the stated basis for the vaccine categories in the executive order. Trump said, “Today, we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s Gold Standard Childhood Vaccination Recommendations and that has to do with many subjects, but including autism in particular.” He later said, “Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthier and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So, there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism. And we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was.”
Existing research does not support a causal link between MMR vaccination and autism. A 2015 study indexed by the National Library of Medicine examined more than 95,000 children and found no association between MMR vaccination and increased autism risk, including among children with an older sibling with autism. CBS News also cited a large 2019 Danish study involving more than 650,000 children that reached a similar conclusion.
Medical groups are also challenging the federal government’s narrower approach. The American Academy of Pediatrics continues to recommend routine vaccination against 18 diseases in its 2026 childhood immunization schedule, rather than limiting its universal recommendations to the 11 diseases included in the new federal framework. The organization has argued that vaccine schedules cannot be copied directly from other nations because countries face different disease risks, demographics, health care systems and vaccine availability.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who is also a physician, offered one of the strongest political rebukes of the Trump vaccine plan. According to CBS News, Cassidy said, “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong.”
For parents, the biggest takeaway is that the Trump vaccine plan does not erase every vaccine outside the 11 disease routine category. Instead, it changes the federal government’s position on which immunizations should be recommended universally, which should depend on elevated risk and which should be discussed individually between families and clinicians. That distinction matters, especially as the administration uses the much larger “72 jabs” figure to sell a policy change that is actually about how vaccines and vaccine preventable diseases are categorized across the federal childhood schedule.

sources.news_title: TPA Slams White House Order Splitting Childhood Vaccines
sources.text:
TPA Slams White House Order Splitting Childhood Vaccines
Taxpayers Protection Alliance
August 10, 2026
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Contact: Kara Zupkus (224) 456-0257
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the White House announced a new executive order (EO) that would overhaul the federal childhood immunization schedule. Among its provisions, the EO pushes to break up the combined measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) shot into three standalone doses given at separate appointments.
In response to the release of the EO, Ross Marchand, Executive Director of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance, offered the following statement:
“Once again, the federal government is trying to insert itself between millions of patients and lifesaving vaccines. While it may sound tempting or intuitive to space out childhood vaccines, separating out the combined MMR vaccine into individual components increases the length of time children remain unprotected during their most vulnerable developmental months. Delaying protections for the most vulnerable children is a recipe for preventable suffering. Further, single-antigen vaccines for mumps and rubella are no longer manufactured or available in the U.S., making attempts to split the dose logistically complex and practically impossible. Requiring multiple doctor visits instead of a single injection also increases healthcare costs and barriers, leading to higher rates of delayed doses or missed immunizations altogether.
“Despite the branding, these changes are more than just altered ‘recommendations.’ For starters, any president’s recommendation or executive order carries immense weight with agency heads and citizens. Changing the schedule also has profound legal consequences, exposing vaccine manufacturers to runaway litigation and threatening access to lifesaving products for millions of Americans. Whether a vaccine is on or off the childhood vaccine schedule directly impacts its exposure to oft-frivolous litigation.
“In a perfect world, federal vaccine recommendations wouldn’t be so important in determining which vaccines will be sued out of existence. But because the childhood vaccine schedule is such an important gatekeeper of patient choice, policymakers should do everything in their power to maintain patient access and choice. It is time to finally move away from the irresponsible Make America Healthy Again movement’s anti-vaccine hysterics.”
A recent poll conducted by Echelon Insights and released by TPA highlighted that Americans want continued access to vaccines and vaccine recommendations free from political influence – with 91% saying it is important that families retain access to safe, FDA-approved vaccines
###
The Taxpayers Protection Alliance (TPA) is a non-profit, non-partisan organization dedicated to educating the public through the research, analysis, and dissemination of information on the government’s impact on the economy.

sources.news_title: Trump calls for spacing out MMR vaccine into three shots, suggests it causes autism
President Mandates Sweeping Changes to Childhood Vaccination Schedule
sources.text:
President Mandates Sweeping Changes to Childhood Vaccination Schedule
                     
                
                WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday directing federal health officials to dramatically revise the government’s childhood vaccine recommendations, mandating fewer routine shots and separate doctor’s visits for some immunizations.
Significantly, the order would recommend that the combined MMR vaccine be divided into three separate shots when such vaccines become available in the United States.
Currently, separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not licensed for use in this country.
Speaking to reporters as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Deputy Assistant to the President of Domestic Policy Dr. Heidi Overton looked on, the president said the order was intended to give parents more flexibility and to reduce the number of vaccines given to young children at one time.
“One year with five separate visits is better than all the shots in one visit,” Trump said.
A White House fact sheet said the order calls for “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” and directs federal health agencies to improve vaccine research.
It also advises states with school vaccine requirements to consider changes reflecting the administration’s recommendations.
States and local governments, not the federal government, generally set vaccination requirements for school attendance.
The order follows earlier administration efforts to revise the childhood immunization schedule.
In January, Kennedy announced that HHS would seek to reduce the number of diseases for which all children are routinely vaccinated.
A federal judge blocked those changes in March, saying the government had not followed proper scientific procedures.
Kennedy later removed all 17 members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and appointed new members, several of whom have questioned vaccine policy or vaccine mandates.
The same judge who acted on Kennedy’s earlier proposal suspended 13 of the new members and voided prior votes taken by the panel.
The CDC advisory committee traditionally reviews vaccine safety and effectiveness data and recommends immunization schedules for children and adults. The White House order seeks to direct federal agencies to revise those recommendations.
Public health officials and medical groups have said childhood vaccines and combination shots are studied before approval and are monitored after they go into widespread use.
They have warned that spacing out vaccines could leave children susceptible to preventable diseases if families miss later appointments.
The order comes as many schools are opening for the year and as health officials monitor a measles outbreak. Experts have said continued spread could threaten the nation’s measles elimination status.
The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning the disease was no longer spreading continuously in the country. Outbreaks since then have generally been linked to travel and communities with low vaccination rates.
Trump again referred Monday to his belief that vaccines may be linked to autism. He said “bad things happen” when multiple vaccines are given close together and referred to autism as “an explosion” and “an epidemic.”
Scientific studies over several decades have found no link between childhood vaccines and autism.
Kennedy said Monday that he believes an unknown environmental factor may be connected to rising autism diagnoses and said HHS would release research findings “as soon as they are ready.”
The order also directs federal agencies to review childhood immunization practices in other developed nations, according to the White House. Trump issued a similar directive in December.
Under the order, six vaccines would continue to receive full routine recommendations for children, according to administration descriptions.
Several others, including hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, would be moved to categories requiring individual risk assessments or shared decision-making between doctors and parents.
The administration also said vaccines for some diseases would be recommended only for high-risk children. Those include vaccines or treatments related to respiratory syncytial virus, meningococcal disease and dengue.
Opponents said the order would place political direction above scientific review.
Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J., ranking Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the order would allow political appointees to overrule “decades of peer-reviewed science.” He said parents need medical guidance from independent experts.
Protect Our Care, a health advocacy group, said spacing out shots would increase the risk that children miss follow-up appointments and remain exposed to disease.
“If Trump’s baseless, science-free decree is followed, the end result will not be fewer children with autism, but far more in the ER or even the morgue,” said Anne Shoup, a senior advisor to the group. “Whether or not state health departments follow Trump’s ignorant guidance, this official proclamation from the highest level of power will have a further chilling effect on vaccination rates across the board.”
The White House said the order was designed to increase parental choice and strengthen confidence in vaccine research.
Administration officials did not immediately say how soon HHS would issue revised recommendations or whether manufacturers would seek approval for separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines.
Licensing separate shots could take years under existing regulatory procedures.

President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order directing the federal government to pursue significant changes to the nation’s childhood vaccination recommendations, including separating combination vaccines and spacing out shots over multiple medical visits.
The order calls for the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine to be administered as three separate shots when individual vaccines become available in the United States. It also recommends that, to the greatest extent feasible, childhood immunizations be administered at separate medical appointments rather than together.
In a statement, the White House said the order is intended to promote greater parental choice and improve vaccine research. It directs the Department of Health and Human Services to reassess the timing and sequencing of childhood vaccines and advance additional research into vaccines and autism.
The move represents a major shift in federal vaccine policy and comes as the school year begins in many parts of the country and the United States faces a significant measles outbreak.
Trump has for years questioned whether the number and timing of childhood vaccinations could contribute to autism. Those concerns have persisted despite decades of research and a broad scientific consensus that vaccines do not cause autism. Studies have examined both individual vaccines and the effects of receiving multiple vaccines according to recommended schedules.
The order follows months of debate within the Trump administration over childhood immunizations. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a long history of questioning vaccine policies, has pushed for changes to the federal vaccination schedule. Vaccine advisers appointed by Kennedy previously recommended separating the MMR vaccine into individual shots.
The administration’s actions also follow an earlier effort to reduce the number of vaccines recommended for children. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in January recommended reducing the number of childhood vaccinations for certain diseases, while the American Academy of Pediatrics maintained recommendations covering a broader range of childhood diseases. A federal judge later blocked the CDC’s proposed changes.
The executive order does not itself eliminate state vaccination requirements for students. States continue to determine which vaccines children must receive to attend public schools, although federal recommendations can influence medical practice, insurance coverage and public health policy.
One of the most consequential changes proposed by the order involves the MMR vaccine. The combined vaccine protects children against measles, mumps and rubella with a single series of shots. Separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are not currently available for children in the United States, meaning the administration’s recommendation would depend on the availability of individual vaccines.
Medical experts have raised concerns that requiring additional appointments could make it more difficult for children to receive all recommended doses. More appointments create additional opportunities for missed visits or delayed vaccinations, potentially increasing the period during which children remain unprotected.
Although recommendations from the C.D.C. greatly influence state regulations, states, not the federal government, have the authority to mandate vaccinations.
